items.title: Nigeria must leverage digital infrastructure to expand economic opportunities – Expert

original_payload.original_title: Nigeria must leverage digital infrastructure to expand economic opportunities – Expert
original_payload.original_body:
General News  Nigeria must leverage digital infrastructure to expand economic opportunities – Expert
By  Nefisetu Yakubu   ·   1 hour ago   ·  3 min read
✓
✓
By Usman Aliyu
A digital technology expert, Robert Karanja, has called on Nigeria to leverage its growing digital public infrastructure to expand economic opportunities, attract investment and deepen financial inclusion.
Karanja spoke in an interview with the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) in Balaclava, Mauritius, on the sidelines of the launch of the 2026 State of Inclusive Instant Payment Systems (SIIPS) in Africa Report.
According to him, the country’s progress in digital payments, identity management and data exchange provides a foundation for accelerating economic growth through technology-driven services.
Karanja, who is an expert in Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI), said Nigeria’s experience in developing inclusive digital payment systems offered valuable lessons for other African countries seeking to build infrastructure that supported economic activities.
He said Nigeria’s instant payment infrastructure, operated by the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System (NIBSS), remained a significant achievement in Africa’s digital transformation journey.
“Nigeria has also made progress in digital identity and data exchange, which can further strengthen the country’s digital economy when effectively integrated,” he said.
He, however, said the impact of digital infrastructure should be assessed by how much it improved people’s economic activities and livelihoods.
Karanja, who is the founder of DPI4Africa, said affordability of internet connectivity, mobile data and electricity remained critical challenges that could limit the ability of Nigerians to benefit fully from digital services.
He said that addressing the challenges would require sustained investment in infrastructure and policies that made digital platforms accessible to individuals, businesses and underserved communities.
The expert said Nigeria could also benefit from stronger collaboration between government and the private sector in developing and deploying digital public infrastructure.
He said the Africa DPI Private Sector Coalition, which he also currently leads, brought  together major financial institutions, telecommunications companies and fintechs, was established to provide the private sector with a stronger voice in the development of digital infrastructure.
“The coalition has attracted eight major institutions and is targeting 20 members, with a focus on promoting investment, developing use cases and supporting the adoption of digital public infrastructure,” Karanja said.
Nigeria, he said, was already contributing to the initiative, with NIBSS among the institutions participating in the coalition.
According to him, the private sector’s involvement will  help ensure that digital infrastructure is designed to respond to practical economic needs and support businesses.
Karanja said Nigeria should also explore ways of measuring the economic impact of digital infrastructure beyond the number of people registered on digital platforms.
He said growth in small businesses, increased commercial activities, improved access to markets and opportunities for rural communities could provide better indicators of the effectiveness of digital transformation.
The expert said expanding access to digital services could help businesses reach more customers, improve transactions and create opportunities for people outside major urban centres.
He said digital infrastructure should ultimately support economic activities, improve livelihoods and enable more Nigerians to participate in the country’s digital economy.
(NAN)

original_payload.original_title: World ​‌‌‍‌⁠​‍⁠⁠‍‍⁠​‍​⁠‍‍‌​Children’s Day: UNICEF seeks action on children’s rights, safety
original_payload.original_body:
General News  World ​‌‌‍‌⁠​‍⁠⁠‍‍⁠​‍​⁠‍‍‌​Children’s Day: UNICEF seeks action on children’s rights, safety
By  Nefisetu Yakubu   ·   2 hours ago   ·  4 min read
✓
✓
By Millicent Ifeanyichukwu
The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) has tasked governments and stakeholders to create an enabling environment that will translate children’s aspirations into concrete actions.
The organisation says that such will ensure the children’s rights, safety and future.
UNICEF Lagos Chief of Field Office Celine Lafoucriere gave the charge in her address at an event to commemorate the 2026 World Children’s Day (WCD) in Lagos on Friday.
Lafoucriere said that children’s rights to safety, healthcare, education and participation in decisions affecting their lives were fundamental entitlements, not privileges to be granted by adults.
She said that the 2026 theme, ‘My Day, My Rights, My Future’, provided an opportunity to listen to children’s experiences, aspirations and expectations for a better society.
‘’When our children paint the Nigeria they dream of, our job as adults is not to admire the picture. Our job is to build it,” she said.
She urged adults to pay attention to the children’s messages during the gallery walk and make practical commitments toward addressing the issues raised in their artworks.
Lafoucriere said that UNICEF would document the commitments made by stakeholders and follow up to ensure they translated into meaningful actions for children.
She said that UNICEF was synergising with the Lagos State Government to ensure every child enjoyed access to education, healthcare, adequate nutrition, clean water, sanitation and social protection, irrespective of background.
The UNICEF officer said that social protection programmes were essential to preventing vulnerable children from being excluded from basic services.
According to her, recognition of children’s rights must translate into practical support for their daily needs.
‘’Having a right is one thing, but it does not necessarily put food on the table.
‘’Social protection ensures vulnerable children can access education, healthcare, good nutrition and clean water,” she said.
She appreciated the Lagos State Ministry of Youth and Social Development; Lagos State Children’s Parliament; Young People Action Team; teachers and parents for supporting the celebration.
In his remark, Mr Mobolaji Ogunlende, Commissioner, Youth and Social Development said that the government was prioritising children’s rights and future through the THEMES Plus Agenda.
Ogunlende identified the importance of partnerships in improving children’s welfare and development, saying, ‘’The government cannot do it alone.
‘’Children must understand their rights and aspirations, while government, parents and stakeholders should provide the necessary foundation to help them achieve their dreams.
‘’We must continue to build partnerships and collaborations to ensure that we give our children the future they deserve, being the reason we are identifying with UNICEF organised event,’’.
He thanked UNICEF for its continued collaboration and commitment to the wellbeing of children, assured the children that their voices would continue beyond the celebration, adding, “the ministry must translate what was heard at the event into meaningful actions and commitments,”.
Also speaking, Speaker of the Lagos State Children’s Parliament, Anjola Abdulsalam, called for increased investment in education, inclusion of children with special needs and participation in decisions affecting their lives.
Abdulsalam stressed the need to ensure every child accessed quality education, while creating platforms for children to share experiences, report abuse and contribute meaningfully to policies affecting their welfare.
“Government must invest more in children’s education, ensure children with special needs are not excluded and create opportunities for our voices to influence decisions affecting our lives,” she said
The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the World Children’s Day is observed annually on Nov. 20 to promote international togetherness, awareness of children’s rights and improvement of their welfare.
The day commemorates the adoption of the Declaration of the Rights of the Child by the United Nations General Assembly on Nov. 20, 1959, and the Convention on the Rights of the Child on Nov. 20, 1989.
The convention, a landmark international human rights treaty, recognises every child’s rights to survival, development, protection and participation, regardless of background or circumstances. (NAN)

items.title: Tinubu’s Ibadan rally: Transport operators lament restrictions as petty traders record brisk business

original_payload.original_title: Tinubu’s Ibadan rally: Transport operators lament restrictions as petty traders record brisk business
original_payload.original_body:
COMMERCIAL transport operators and petty traders around Mapo Hall in Ibadan, Oyo State, are recording contrasting experiences as restrictions on vehicular movement and heavy security deployment accompanied President Bola Tinubu’s presidential campaign rally on Saturday.
While some tricycle and motorcycle operators complained that the restrictions prevented them from accessing certain parts of the city, affecting their ability to pick up passengers and make daily earnings, petty traders around the rally venue said the increased human traffic had boosted their businesses.
The restrictions were imposed around Mapo Hall, Beere and adjoining roads as security operatives took control of the area ahead of Tinubu’s visit for the All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential campaign rally.
The ICIR  observed a heavy presence of security personnel at strategic locations around Mapo, with some roads leading to the venue barricaded and vehicular movement restricted.
The development forced many residents to trek to their destinations, while others walked towards the rally venue to join the gathering.

items.title: After years of alleged plastic pollution, dust settles for Niger community

original_payload.original_title: After years of alleged plastic pollution, dust settles for Niger community
original_payload.original_body:
By Hamzat Ibrahim ABAGA
Residents of Gidan Madara, a residential community near Minna, the Niger State capital, can now breathe fresh air and sleep peacefully at night. Years of alleged air and noise pollution from Golden Age Hi-Tech and Production Company, a plastic-melting and recycling factory that operated its equipment and machinery around the clock, came to a stop when a Chief Magistrate Court II in Minna ordered the company to relocate its activities.
Before then, residents claimed that pollution emanating from the factory may have caused illnesses that resulted in deaths in the community. They had made several complaints in the past, including a petition to the Niger State Environmental Protection Agency (NISEPA), which eventually sparked a legal dispute over the factory’s operations within the neighbourhood.
The ICIR,  which monitored the tension while the case was before the court, spoke with many residents who said the company began as a sachet and bottled water producer in October 2013 before expanding into plastic melting at the same premises in  2019 .
Residents said they had no complaints about the firm when it engaged solely in water production. But things changed when they began experiencing breathing difficulties and other health problems after the company expanded into plastic melting and recycling.

items.title: 16 killed, 10 injured in W. Kordofan shelter drone strike

original_payload.original_title: 16 killed, 10 injured in W. Kordofan shelter drone strike
original_payload.original_body:
At least 16 internally displaced people were killed and 10 others injured on Tuesday night when a drone allegedly belonging to the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) struck a displacement shelter in Ghubaysh, West Kordofan State.
A statement by Kordofan Observatory, which was extended to Radio Tamazuj, accused the SAF of escalating attacks that endanger civilian lives, saying the strike targeted Musab bin Umair Western School, which was sheltering hundreds of people displaced by fighting around the town of En Nuhud.
“In a dangerous escalation by the Sudanese army that threatens civilian lives, a drone struck Musab bin Umair Western School at approximately 8 p.m. on Tuesday,” the statement read. “The school was sheltering hundreds of displaced people who had fled the conflict around En Nuhud.”
Imad Abdel Hadi, Executive Director of Ghubaysh Locality, told the publication that the Sudanese army had repeatedly used drone strikes against towns and populated areas, spreading fear among civilians.
He alleged that the army had previously targeted Abu Galb, Abu Zabad and En Nuhud, adding that Ghubaysh had come under successive drone attacks for three consecutive days.
Meanwhile, Mohamed Hamid, a resident of Ghubaysh Locality, described the situation as deeply distressing, citing repeated drone strikes on markets, residential neighborhoods and schools.
“On Tuesday night, an army drone struck a school near my home in Ghubaysh, firing three projectiles and killing several displaced people, including children and elderly residents,” Hamid said.
Hamid called on the Sudanese army to respect the civilian status of schools, markets, and residential areas and to take precautions to protect civilian infrastructure and lives when carrying out military operations.

items.title: Panic in Damazin amid military operations in Bau, Geissan

original_payload.original_title: Panic in Damazin amid military operations in Bau, Geissan
original_payload.original_body:
The inhabitants of Damazin, the capital of Sudan’s Blue Nile State, are experiencing mounting anxiety and uncertainty following recent military battles in Bau and Geissan localities, amid fears that the fighting could escalate and spread to other parts of the region.
According to local sources, forces affiliated with the Tasis Alliance have advanced into Bau locality and seized control of the Taga area. The alliance’s forces have also reportedly captured Madina 11 in Geissan locality, developments that have heightened concerns about the region’s deteriorating security situation.
The reported advances have cast a shadow over Damazin, where residents remain apprehensive about the possibility of hostilities spreading to other areas. The lack of clear information about ongoing military operations and their potential consequences has further compounded public anxiety.
Elham Kamal, a resident of Damazin, described the security situation as extremely complex, saying some residents had already fled the city while others had been forced to remain because they could not afford the cost of travelling to safer areas.
Civil society activist Ehab Al-Sir said the latest military developments had intensified fear and uncertainty among residents, leaving many in a state of constant trepidation.
“We call on the government and relevant authorities to provide clear and reliable information about the security situation and to take concrete measures to protect civilians,” he said.
Al-Sir also urged the authorities to prepare for possible further military developments and potential waves of displacement.
Radio Tamazuj was unable to obtain a comment from government authorities regarding the latest military developments or the growing security concerns and their implications for residents of Damazin.
The mounting fears come against the backdrop of an increasingly complex security and humanitarian situation across the Blue Nile Region, raising questions about the potential repercussions of the fighting in Bau and Geissan for the safety and stability of Damazin and surrounding areas.
Fighting continues between the Sudanese Armed Forces and allied forces on one side and the Tasis Alliance on the other in several parts of the region, including Kurmuk, Geissan, Bau, and Wad Al-Mahi localities.
Local sources also reported fresh military developments in the Taga area earlier today, further fueling concerns about the trajectory of the conflict and its potential impact on civilian communities.

items.title: Sudan’s Khatmiyya order names new spiritual leader

original_payload.original_title: Sudan’s Khatmiyya order names new spiritual leader
original_payload.original_body:
The family of late Sudanese religious and political leader Mohamed Osman al-Mirghani has appointed his eldest son, Ali, as the new spiritual leader of the Khatmiyya Sufi order, leaving the leadership of his political party unresolved.
The appointment settles the succession at the helm of one of Sudan’s largest Sufi orders but leaves open a potentially contentious contest for control of the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) between two of al-Mirghani’s other sons, Mohamed al-Hassan and Jaafar al-Sadiq.
Announcing the family’s decision on Friday, Jaafar al-Sadiq said the siblings had agreed to rally behind their eldest brother and support his leadership of the religious order.
“My brothers and I are the first to stand behind him, support him, and place our hands in his to serve the order and its people,” Jaafar said.
In his first address as spiritual leader, Ali al-Mirghani urged followers to resolve differences through dialogue, respect opposing views and reject division. He also called for greater efforts towards reconciliation and unity.
Ali has lived in the United States since the mid-1990s.  His father died  in Cairo last Friday and was buried on Monday at the Sayyid Ali al-Mirghani Mosque in Khartoum North.
Political divisions
Rivalry over the DUP leadership emerged during Mohamed Osman al-Mirghani’s lifetime, when Mohamed al-Hassan and Jaafar al-Sadiq clashed over the influential position of deputy chairman for organizational affairs.
Their differences have been deepened by their opposing positions on Sudan’s war, which began in April 2023 between the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
Mohamed al-Hassan has aligned himself with anti-war civilian forces, while Jaafar al-Sadiq has supported the Sudanese army in the conflict, highlighting divisions within the family over the country’s political and military crisis.

items.title: The TPLF’s Setbacks Do Not Determine Tigray’s Political Future

original_payload.original_title: The TPLF’s Setbacks Do Not Determine Tigray’s Political Future
original_payload.original_body:
Viewpoint
The TPLF’s Setbacks Do Not Determine Tigray’s Political Future
21 November, 2026
Selam Tesfay
SUPPORT ETHIOPIA INSIGHT
Both the party and the federal government must earn public trust through reform and delivery
What lies ahead for Tigray? Some, particularly  officials  of the federal government and  Tigray Peace Force  (TPF), believe the TPLF is finished. TPLF and TDF leaders, however, present a different narrative. While both emphasize the possibility of a comeback,  some  acknowledge temporary territorial losses, while others  characterize  the withdrawal as a strategic retreat.
These competing narratives overlook two more important questions: What explains the TPLF’s recent setbacks, and what will determine Tigray’s political future?
I argue that the TPLF’s defeat is primarily a political leadership failure, reflected in at least five major miscalculations. Its future, however, is not settled. Much will depend on what the federal government and the TPLF do next.
Political Miscalculations
After years of devastating conflict, the people of Tigray are exhausted by war. This reality is evident even to an ordinary observer, yet it appears not to have been adequately reflected in the TPLF leadership’s calculations. The leadership seems to have underestimated the people’s desire for peace, recovery, and normal life.
Unlike the 2020–2022 war, which was largely  understood  as a war on Tigray by external forces, the recent conflict has a strong internal dimension. It reflects divisions between those in power and Tigrayans who feel excluded, marginalized, or unheard.
In my assessment, internal dissatisfaction and its mishandling contributed more to the TPLF’s defeat than the federal government’s military strength. Federal involvement mattered, but internal divisions and declining political support were more decisive. Presenting this conflict as just another war for Tigray’s survival therefore risks misreading its nature. Internal grievances cannot be overcome simply by invoking an external threat.
Historically, the TPLF relied heavily on persuasion to recruit fighters, while generally leaving the final decision to the individual. During the recent conflict, reported  forced conscription , backed by harsh laws, marked a significant departure from that tradition. Reports of mothers being  detained  and pressured to produce their children for recruitment disappointed many. Pointing to compulsory national service elsewhere does not resolve questions of individual rights, public consent, and political legitimacy.
The TPLF also appears to have underestimated the international support Abiy Ahmed’s government could mobilize. Ethiopia’s strategic location, regional importance, and position on the Nile give it considerable geopolitical influence.
Publicly  declaring  an intention to remove Abiy from power, whether as a genuine objective, domestic rhetoric, or an attempt to pressure him, also raises questions about whether the diplomatic consequences were carefully considered.
The leadership appears to have underestimated the adversary’s technology, financial resources, manpower, and ability to sustain conflict. Despite receiving cautionary advice, it also seems to have overestimated the support available from the “Alliance for Survival.”
Misjudging an opponent’s strength while placing excessive confidence in allies can lead to unrealistic strategies and costly setbacks.
Taken together, these failures suggest that the TPLF’s defeat was not simply the result of superior military force. It was fundamentally a political leadership failure, manifested in poor judgment and a growing disconnect from the people.
Federal Responsibilities
The TPLF’s setbacks do not necessarily settle Tigray’s political future. Neither its complete disappearance nor a comeback can be ruled out entirely.
I argue that the outcome will depend mainly on how the federal government and the TPLF respond to the people’s needs and aspirations.
If the federal government delivers peace, humanitarian relief, resettlement, development, and democratic self-government while the TPLF continues to repeat its mistakes, the party’s decline could deepen. Conversely, if the government fails to deliver while the TPLF reforms, conditions for renewed support could emerge. The main tests facing the federal government are clear.
Peace must come first. Military gains should not be mistaken for the end of the war. Reports of senior TPLF politicians and  commanders  surrendering suggest that the organization is weakening, but the risk of continued instability remains. Declaring the war over does not make it so.
The federal government should therefore seek a negotiated settlement with the leadership, creating a path from armed struggle to peaceful political participation. Success means ending the cycle of war, not merely defeating an armed opponent.
The federal government should distinguish between criticism of the TPLF’s political leadership and attacks on Tigray’s history and collective legacy. Tigrayans’ historical experiences, including the struggle in which the TPLF played a central role, remain important to many people, even among those who disagree with the party’s current leadership. Political messaging that targets Tigrayan history and identity could turn dissatisfaction with the party into solidarity with it.
People urgently need food, medicine, and essential services. Humanitarian assistance should receive the same urgency as security operations and should not wait for the completion of disarmament, demobilization, and reintegration (DDR). Success should be measured by assistance actually reaching hungry families, patients, and displaced communities, not by announcements.
The return of displaced people, particularly those from Western Tigray, is essential to lasting peace. The federal government should address territorial disputes through peaceful and constitutional means while taking immediate steps to ensure security, disarm armed elements threatening returnees, and address the occupation of displaced families’ homes and farmland.
Peace must bring visible economic improvement, particularly for young people. The federal government should restart major projects suspended during the war and launch new investments, including infrastructure rehabilitation and job-creating initiatives. Restored services, functioning infrastructure, and employment opportunities would give people tangible reasons to believe in peace.
The federal government must understand that Tigrayans seek political agency, the right to shape their own future, administer their affairs, and freely choose their leaders. Respecting Tigray’s constitutional right to self-government is therefore essential. Imposing political leadership from outside risks reviving grievances.
But self-government should not mean returning power to one party. Tigray needs a broad political framework, a big tent, where all parties participate and compete under equal rules, without special privileges. The federal government’s role should be to enable this process, not determine its outcome.
TPLF’s Choices
The TPLF must reconsider whether its current leadership can respond to the new political reality. In my assessment, a meaningful recovery under the current leadership would be difficult. New leadership must bring better judgment, public acknowledgment of past mistakes and a better vision for Tigray’s future. Replacing individuals without political reform would achieve little.
The TPLF must also recognize that the people do not want another war. Continued fighting would exacerbate suffering and could further weaken its political standing. It should pursue every credible opportunity for a negotiated settlement rather than assume that renewed confrontation will restore its former position.
The party should recognize that its former near-exclusive control over Tigray’s political, military, and administrative institutions cannot simply be assumed to return. Its future should be as a civilian political party competing peacefully with others. Its strength must come from its political program and ability to win votes, not military power, media control, or privileged access to government resources. Political authority must be earned through elections, not inherited from past struggles.
The TPLF must distinguish between the interests of its leaders, the party, and the people of Tigray. If it claims to represent the people, it must recognize that endless war cannot serve their interests. It should address internal grievances, accept necessary compromises, and seize credible opportunities for peace, even at the cost of reduced political power. The question is not how the TPLF can restore its former dominance, but how it can contribute to Tigray’s peace and recovery.
The party must also better understand the strategic interests and priorities of the international community. Diplomacy requires realistic judgment, not wishful thinking.
It must reassess its relationships with external forces whose interests may not align with those of Tigray. Depending on such alliances could undermine its credibility, limit diplomatic opportunities, and complicate prospects for peace. The TPLF’s diplomatic strategy should be guided by Tigray’s long-term interests, not by the agendas of external powers.
The TPLF’s recent setbacks raise serious questions about its leadership and strategic judgment. But military defeat alone will not determine its political future, just as military victory will not guarantee the federal government’s success.
The federal government’s challenge is to turn military gains into peace, humanitarian relief, reconstruction, and democratic self-government. The TPLF’s challenge is to learn from its mistakes, renew itself, reassess its external alliances, and accept a role based on public consent rather than military or institutional power.
Ultimately, Tigray’s future will depend less on who claims victory today than on who earns the people’s trust through concrete actions. Military power may determine who controls territory, but only political legitimacy and public confidence can sustain peace.

original_payload.original_title: Sécurité routière : La Brigade active retire les phares non conformes sur l’axe nord de N’Djaména.
original_payload.original_body:
Sécurité routière : La Brigade active retire les phares non conformes sur l’axe nord de N’Djaména.
admin
novembre 21, 2026
2 minutes lues
110 vues
Sur l’axe nord de N’Djaména, la Brigade active de la sécurité routière de l’Office National de la Sécurité Routière (ONASER) a mené ce 20 novembre 2026, une opération de retrait des phares non conformes installés sur les véhicules de transport.
Composée d’éléments de la Police nationale et de la Gendarmerie nationale travaillant aux côtés des équipes de l’ONASER, la Brigade active de sécurité routière a été lancée officiellement le 2 septembre 2026.
Présent lors de cette opération, le directeur de la Brigade active, Ahmat Ramadane Guirsidé a rappelé que cette descente a pour objectif de vérifier et de retirer systématiquement les phares non conformes, conformément aux décisions prises par les autorités.
«  Nous avions convenu avec les syndicats des transporteurs d’un délai de deux semaines avant que les actions ne soient menées sur le terrain. Ce délai étant épuisé, nous sommes aujourd’hui descendus pour le retrait systématique de ces équipements  », a-t-il martelé.
Ahmat Ramadane Guirsidé a ensuite ajouté que cette opération s’est déroulée dans de bonnes conditions et sans aucune résistance .Il a ensuite profité pour saluer également la coopération des usagers de la route et des conducteurs de poids lourds.
TWM/ Mahamat Moussa Ahmadou

original_payload.original_title: Salubrité publique : la Commune du 1er arrondissement passe à l’action à Guinebor 1
original_payload.original_body:
La Commune du 1er arrondissement a lancé, ce samedi 21 novembre 2026, une journée de salubrité au quartier Guinebor 1. La cérémonie de lancement a été présidée par le ministre des Infrastructures, du Désenclavement et de l’Entretien routier, Amir Idriss Kourda, en présence de plusieurs responsables communaux, dont le maire adjoint du 1er arrondissement Mahamat HassanaMahamat.

items.title: Riemann hypothesis: Has the world’s most famous maths problem been cracked?

original_payload.original_title: Riemann hypothesis: Has the world’s most famous maths problem been cracked?
original_payload.original_body:
A mathematician from the AI giant  Anthropic  claims to have proven one of the world’s most famous – and most elusive – maths problems.
Levent Alpoge wrote on his website on Friday: “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.”
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items    list 1 of 3  California files lawsuit against OpenAI alleging lack of proper safeguards
list 2 of 3  AI models abandon climate facts to please users, UNESCO report finds
list 3 of 3  China’s DeepSeek unveils latest models a year after upending global tech
end of list
If his claim holds up, the proof he says he has would settle a question that has defeated mathematicians for 167 years. Independent experts are now trying to verify it, but so far no human has read through the entire argument.
Here is what we know.
What is the Riemann hypothesis?
First proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and is widely regarded as the most important open question in pure mathematics.
Prime numbers are whole numbers which can be divided only by one and themselves, such as 2, 3, 5 and 7. They appear to be scattered along the number line with no obvious pattern but the Riemann hypothesis proposes that their overall distribution actually follows a deep, hidden order – just one that humans have yet to identify.
“The Riemann hypothesis is the most famous and important unsolved problem in mathematics,” Abhishek Saha, professor of mathematics at Queen Mary University of London, told Al Jazeera.
“The patterns of the primes are encoded in a mathematical object called the Riemann zeta function, introduced by Bernhard Riemann in 1859.”
It is one of the seven Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, each carrying a $1m award.
What has the Anthropic mathematician claimed?
Alpoge, a member of the company’s technical staff, made the announcement on Friday in a four-page explanation posted on his website. He said the proof he has found covers the generalised Riemann hypothesis, which extends the original conjecture to a broader family of mathematical functions.

items.title: Sudan’s elderly face hardship and heartbreak in a life of displacement

original_payload.original_title: Sudan’s elderly face hardship and heartbreak in a life of displacement
original_payload.original_body:
Khartoum, Sudan –  Hamad Mohammed Adam, 70, should be spending his days surrounded by his family and enjoying the comfort of life in his home village. Instead, he finds himself among hundreds of displaced elderly people in a camp in western Omdurman, with little between him and death.
Three months ago, Adam’s life changed when the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary attacked his village near Bara, northern Kordofan. He followed the rest of the village and fled, leaving behind his home, belongings and most painfully, his family.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items    list 1 of 3  Traumas of Sudan war lead to wave of drug addiction
list 2 of 3  Sudan’s war leaves disabled children missing out on education
list 3 of 3  Sudan’s war will end, but will it be too late?
end of list
“It was an early morning last August when the Rapid Support Forces militia invaded our village near Bara. It was a terrifying morning; they were killing everyone, women, men, children,” he said. “I ran with some friends and spent days to reach Omdurman. I am lucky that I have survived, but I am worried about my family.”
The war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the RSF paramilitary, two former military allies now engaged in a bitter power struggle for Sudan since April 2023, has affected all parts of the country. When fighting erupts in one area, residents are often forced to flee to another, where they lack jobs, a home, or a support base.
After travelling for about 300km (186 miles), Adam found himself in western Omdurman, close to the capital Khartoum. Today, he resides at al-Moulih camp for displaced people in western Omdurman, home to approximately 10,000 people, with those aged over 65 accounting for about one in five residents.
His escape from the fighting between the SAF and RSF, which has triggered one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, was only the start of his troubles. Adam knows nothing about the whereabouts of his family, and they don’t know where he is.

items.title: Demolition notices for buildings in Hebron provoke fear among Palestinians

original_payload.original_body:
Hebron, Occupied West Bank –  Amjad al-Qawasmi stood gazing at the eight-storey residential building he constructed 13 years ago in the heart of Hebron. He struggled to understand how it could be reduced to rubble in a matter of moments.
The building in the southern West Bank is one of two upon which the Israeli army posted demolition notices last Sunday morning, even though both are in Area A, which, under the Oslo Accords, is under full Palestinian control.

The buildings are in the Dairat al-Seer area, in the northwest of Hebron. One contains 25 residential apartments, the other has 40, alongside an adjacent home. The Israeli army has set a one-week deadline for filing objections to the demolition orders.
The Israeli authorities  justified the decisions  by citing the buildings’ proximity to “Settler Road 35”, despite the structures possessing all the necessary permits from the Palestinian Authority and the Hebron Municipality.
Hebron is divided into a larger area under Palestinian administrative control and a smaller area – housing Israeli settlers – in the centre of the city.
Pervasive fear
The affected families are living in a state of anxiety, fearing that the demolition orders will be carried out. Meanwhile, the property owners have filed formal objections in an attempt to halt the demolitions.
Al-Qawasmi told Al Jazeera that his building was constructed in 2013 at a cost exceeding 18 million shekels ($5.6m). He, along with his father and brother, had prepared the apartments for occupancy from the ground up, installing all necessary utilities after obtaining the required permits from the Ministry of Local Government.

Later on Saturday, the IRGC also claimed bringing down an MQ-1 drone over Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, the 19th such downing.
There was no immediate comment by the US military.
The incidents come days after the US and Iran engaged in  direct, tit-for-tat strikes , against a backdrop of increasing Iranian attacks on vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway through which one-fifth of the world’s oil and gas passed in peacetime.
Launched by the US and Israel on February 28, the war has killed thousands of people and severely disrupted shipping, pushing global energy prices higher and spreading to countries across the region.
The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June, but it was never fully implemented because of disagreements over freedom and security of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, with attacks resuming periodically since July. In August, The Washington Post reported that the US had lost 45 MQ-9 drones, or about 25 percent of its fleet at a cost of more than $1.3bn, during combat operations in Iran.
original_payload.original_summary: Iran reiterates conditions for Hormuz reopening as US slaps sanctions on four Iranians it says acted as 'oil trustees'.

original_payload.original_body:

Cette descente cible particulièrement les gros porteurs et les camions de transport dont de nombreux chauffeurs ont pris l’habitude d’installer des projecteurs additionnels, des rampes LED ou des feux de forte intensité non réglementaires.
L’opération fait suite à de multiples plaintes de citoyens et d’automobilistes, régulièrement aveuglés et mis en danger lors des croisements nocturnes.

items.title: Tchad : le Collectif 2M dresse son bilan des deux premières années du mandat présidentiel

original_payload.original_title: Tchad : le Collectif 2M dresse son bilan des deux premières années du mandat présidentiel
original_payload.original_body:
A l’approche de la mi-mandat du président de la République, le Collectif 2M « Marchons avec Mahamat », dirigé par Senoussi Hassana Abdoulaye, a organisé, ce jeudi 19 novembre 2026 à N’Djaména, une rencontre consacrée à l’évaluation des deux premières années de gouvernance du Maréchal Mahamat Idriss Déby Itno. Plus d’une centaine d’associations et d’organisations de la société civile ont pris part aux échanges, qui ont été sanctionnés par la signature d’une tribune sur le bilan présidentiel et les attentes pour les trois prochaines années.
Évaluer les engagements pris par le chef de l’État, examiner les réalisations enregistrées et identifier les défis qui restent à relever. Tels étaient les principaux objectifs de cette rencontre initiée par le Collectif 2M « Marchons avec Mahamat ».
Prenant la parole, le président du collectif, Senoussi Hassana Abdoulaye, a rappelé que les organisations ayant soutenu le Maréchal Mahamat Idriss Déby Itno lors de l’élection présidentielle du 6 mai 2024 ont également un rôle à jouer dans le suivi de la mise en œuvre de son projet de société. Il a notamment insisté sur la nécessité de reconnaître les avancées réalisées, tout en relevant les insuffisances qui appellent des réponses concrètes.
Dans leur déclaration, les responsables du collectif ont salué les initiatives engagées en faveur de la refondation de l’État, du renforcement des institutions républicaines, de la cohésion sociale et de la stabilité nationale. Ils ont, par ailleurs, réaffirmé leur soutien au chef de l’État, tout en plaidant pour une accélération de la mise en œuvre de ses engagements.
Les discussions ont également permis de passer en revue plusieurs préoccupations majeures des populations. La sécurité, l’emploi des jeunes, l’accès à l’eau potable et à l’électricité, l’éducation, la décentralisation et le renforcement des services sociaux de base ont notamment été abordés.
Une attention particulière a été accordée à l’insertion professionnelle des jeunes, à leur accompagnement ainsi qu’à la recherche de solutions durables aux conflits intracommunautaires. Le pouvoir d’achat a également figuré parmi les préoccupations soulevées, notamment en ce qui concerne les attentes des populations autour de la subvention des denrées alimentaires.
À l’issue des échanges, les associations et organisations participantes ont signé une tribune présentant leur appréciation des deux premières années du mandat présidentiel et formulant des recommandations pour les trois prochaines années.
À travers cette initiative, le Collectif 2M entend poursuivre son accompagnement du chef de l’État, tout en appelant à la concrétisation des engagements pris et à des réponses davantage adaptées aux attentes des populations tchadiennes.

items.title: Salamat : concertation autour de la gestion du parc national de Zakouma et de la réserve du Bahr Salamat

original_payload.original_title: Salamat : concertation autour de la gestion du parc national de Zakouma et de la réserve du Bahr Salamat
original_payload.original_body:
Le délégué général du gouvernement auprès de la province du Salamat, Ahmat Choua Rozi, a présidé, ce vendredi 20 novembre 2026, à Djouna, une rencontre consacrée au processus d’élaboration des plans d’aménagement et de gestion (PAG) du parc national de Zakouma (PNZ) et de la réserve de faune du Bahr Salamat (RFBS), ainsi qu’à leurs règlements intérieurs respectifs. Djouna est une localité située à environ 85 kilomètres au sud d’Am-Timan.
Ces assises s’inscrivent dans le cadre des tournées sous-préfectorales de sensibilisation et de concertation autour de l’élaboration et de la validation des documents de gestion des deux aires protégées.
L’élaboration et la validation de ces plans relèvent de la responsabilité conjointe du ministère en charge de l’Environnement et d’African Parks Network (APN). À ce titre, l’implication des autorités de tutelle dans le pilotage technique et institutionnel du processus est jugée essentielle.
Lire aussi :  Le gouvernement installe le Comité technique chargé de l’élaboration des Plans de développement touristique du Parc national de Zakouma et de la Réserve naturelle et culturelle de l’Ennedi
Pour le directeur général du Grand Écosystème du parc national de Zakouma, Cyril Pélissier, l’objectif est de favoriser une appropriation collective du processus d’élaboration des PAG par l’ensemble des parties prenantes. À cet effet, une méthodologie de travail a été élaborée par l’Unité de gestion du parc (UGP), avec l’appui de consultants.
Cette démarche prévoit notamment la collecte et l’analyse des données, ainsi que l’identification des problématiques liées à la gestion des aires protégées.
Elle comprend également l’organisation d’ateliers provinciaux d’information des parties prenantes, des réunions avec l’équipe technique d’appui pour faire le point sur l’avancement du processus participatif et recueillir les avis, ainsi que des tournées sous-préfectorales auprès des communautés riveraines.
Lire aussi :  Interview : ‘’Lutter contre le braconnage, c’est l’affaire de toutes et tous’’, Cyril Pélissier, directeur du parc national de Zakouma
Ces consultations visent à mettre les communautés au courant des enjeux et des options envisagées avant toute prise de décision, afin de favoriser un dialogue éclairé et de faciliter la conclusion d’accords librement consentis.
L’objectif général de ces tournées est de présenter à l’ensemble des parties prenantes les enjeux, les thématiques et les options liés à la conservation et à la gestion durable du parc national de Zakouma et de la réserve de faune du Bahr Salamat.
De manière spécifique, ces consultations doivent permettre d’examiner, d’enrichir et de valider, de façon participative et concertée, les propositions relatives à l’aménagement, à la gouvernance et à la gestion durable des deux aires protégées.
Elles portent notamment sur la composition, les attributions et l’ancrage territorial des structures concernées, ainsi que sur l’identification et la validation des outils nécessaires à la mise en œuvre des PAG et à l’application des règlements intérieurs.

items.title: Moundou : le tribunal renvoie au 27 novembre le verdict sur la légalité de la mise en place de l’exécutif communal

original_payload.original_title: Moundou : le tribunal renvoie au 27 novembre le verdict sur la légalité de la mise en place de l’exécutif communal
original_payload.original_body:
L’affaire opposant six conseillers communaux de la Convention tchadienne pour la paix et le développement (CTPD) à la Commune de Moundou, au sujet de la mise en place de l’actuel exécutif communal, a été examinée ce vendredi 20 novembre 2026 par la chambre administrative du Tribunal de grande instance (TGI) de Moundou. À l’issue des débats et des plaidoiries, le tribunal a mis l’affaire en délibéré au 27 novembre prochain.
L’audience publique a été marquée par des échanges nourris entre les avocats des deux parties. Me Guillaume Allaramadji Rirongarti, conseil des six conseillers communaux requérants, conteste la régularité de la procédure ayant conduit à l’installation de l’actuel exécutif communal. De son côté, Me Gadnodji Prosper, avocat de la Commune de Moundou, défend la légalité de cette mise en place.
Lire aussi :    Moundou : l’exécutif communal sur la sellette
Un désaccord sur la cessation des fonctions de l’ancien maire
Au cœur du contentieux se trouve la légalité du procès-verbal de la session extraordinaire du 16 juin 2026, qui a consacré la mise en place du nouvel exécutif communal.
Pour Me Guillaume Allaramadji Rirongarti, l’ancien maire, Djékaoussem Elon Bondo, demeure légalement le maire de Moundou. Selon lui, aucun acte administratif ou juridique régulier n’a officiellement mis fin à ses fonctions avant l’installation de son successeur, Béassemda Emmanuel.
Une position contestée par Me Gadnodji Prosper. L’avocat de la Commune soutient que l’ancien maire aurait accepté son départ, notamment en refusant de signer le procès-verbal ayant acté la mise en place du nouvel exécutif. Il invoque également une situation exceptionnelle qui aurait nécessité une intervention urgente.
En réponse, Me Guillaume Allaramadji Rirongarti s’appuie sur la loi organique n° 014/CNT/2024 relative à l’organisation des collectivités autonomes. Il dénonce ce qu’il considère comme une violation des règles de compétence et de procédure.
De son côté, le maire actuel a justifié le changement intervenu à la tête de la municipalité par les difficultés qu’aurait connues la gestion précédente. Il a notamment évoqué des accusations de détournement et de corruption, un manque de collaboration, une gestion qu’il qualifie de chaotique ainsi qu’un niveau d’endettement important.
Lire aussi :    Moundou a un nouvel exécutif communal
Les requérants dénoncent plusieurs irrégularités
Dans leurs conclusions en contre-réplique, les six conseillers communaux de la CTPD ont développé plusieurs arguments pour demander l’annulation du procès-verbal contesté.
Le premier concerne la compétence de l’autorité habilitée à mettre fin aux fonctions du maire. S’appuyant sur les articles 117, 119 et 123 de la loi organique n° 014/CNT/2024, les requérants soutiennent que la démission d’office relève du représentant de l’État dans la commune, tandis que la révocation doit être prononcée par décret motivé pris en Conseil des ministres.
Ils affirment qu’aucun acte du représentant de l’État déclarant l’ancien maire démissionnaire d’office, ni aucun décret de révocation, n’a été produit au dossier.
Les requérants contestent également la régularité de la convocation de la session extraordinaire du 16 juin 2026. Selon eux, la Commune n’a pas versé au dossier l’arrêté préfectoral de convocation. Ils estiment en outre que le délai légal de sept jours prévu pour convoquer le Conseil communal n’aurait pas été respecté. Ils font valoir que, selon les explications de la partie adverse, la convocation serait intervenue le jour même de la session.
Autre point soulevé : l’absence du représentant de l’État à cette séance et les conditions de désignation de la personne chargée de présider les travaux. Les requérants contestent notamment la présidence assurée par le maire adjoint, estimant que les règles de remplacement fondées sur l’âge des conseillers communaux n’auraient pas été respectées.
Les six conseillers mettent également en cause les conditions du vote ayant conduit à la désignation du nouvel exécutif communal. Se référant à l’article 116 de la loi organique, ils rappellent que l’élection du maire doit se dérouler au scrutin secret et à la majorité absolue des voix.
Or, selon leurs conclusions, le procès-verbal litigieux fait plutôt état d’une répartition consensuelle et inclusive des postes entre différentes formations politiques, sans préciser clairement les modalités du scrutin, le nombre de suffrages exprimés ni la majorité effectivement obtenue.
La question du quorum constitue un autre motif de contestation. Les requérants relèvent que le nom du conseiller Mbaidessemel Dionadii figure sur le procès-verbal avec la mention « P.O », laissant entendre qu’il aurait été représenté par procuration. Ils rappellent que l’article 111 de la loi organique prévoit, selon leur interprétation, que seuls les conseillers physiquement présents sont pris en compte et que les procurations ne sont pas valables.
Enfin, les demandeurs estiment que les accusations de mauvaise gestion formulées contre l’ancien exécutif ne peuvent, à elles seules, justifier le non-respect des dispositions légales encadrant la cessation des fonctions d’un maire. Ils soutiennent que les mécanismes spécifiques prévus notamment par les articles 121 à 123 auraient dû être engagés si des fautes étaient reprochées à l’ancien maire.
Lire aussi :    Moundou : le parti CTPD dénonce la désignation de Beassemnda Emmanuel comme maire de Moundou
Une demande d’annulation du procès-verbal
Au terme de leurs conclusions, les six conseillers communaux demandent au tribunal de rejeter les arguments de la Commune et de constater l’absence d’un acte légal mettant fin aux fonctions de l’ancien maire.
Ils sollicitent également la reconnaissance des irrégularités qu’ils dénoncent dans la convocation, la présidence et le déroulement de la session extraordinaire du 16 juin 2026, ainsi que dans les conditions du scrutin et du quorum.
En conséquence, ils demandent l’annulation du procès-verbal de cette session extraordinaire et de toutes les opérations de mise en place du nouvel exécutif communal qui en découlent. Ils réclament enfin la condamnation de la Commune de Moundou aux dépens.
Un climat de tensions autour du contentieux
En attendant le délibéré prévu le 27 novembre 2026, cette affaire continue de susciter des réactions dans le paysage politique local.
En coulisses, certains soutiens de l’actuel exécutif communal accusent le président de la CTPD, Laoukein Kourayo Médard, de faire cause commune avec l’ancien exécutif pour déstabiliser l’équipe municipale en place. Des accusations rejetées par des sources proches de la CTPD, qui dénoncent plutôt des manœuvres sur les réseaux sociaux visant, selon elles, à influencer le cours de la procédure judiciaire.
La décision du Tribunal de grande instance de Moundou, attendue le 27 novembre, devra apporter un éclairage juridique sur la régularité de la mise en place de l’actuel exécutif communal.

original_payload.original_title: Ngone Saar dévoile « ADN », un pont musical entre tradition et modernité
original_payload.original_body:
CULTURE
Ngone Saar dévoile « ADN », un pont musical entre tradition et modernité
Le collectif tchadien Ngone Saar a présenté son deuxième album, « ADN ». Composé de 18 titres, ce projet artistique met à l'honneur les valeurs culturelles et l'héritage du pays.
Alwihda Info
21 nov. 2026
Le collectif Ngone Saar a présenté, vendredi 20 novembre, son deuxième album de 18 titres intitulé « ADN ». Dévoilé lors d'une conférence de presse, ce projet artistique se veut un hommage aux valeurs culturelles du Tchad.
Pour le groupe, cet opus va au-delà d'une simple production musicale. Il ambitionne de raconter l'identité tchadienne et de célébrer l'héritage national. À la croisée de la tradition et de la modernité, l'album est le fruit d'un travail de recherche approfondi.
Les artistes expliquent avoir multiplié les échanges avec des sages et des aînés pour recueillir leurs conseils. Cette démarche de transmission intergénérationnelle a guidé la conception de l'œuvre.
Le collectif garde le secret sur le contenu musical précis, mais donne rendez-vous au public le 27 novembre prochain à Pili Pili pour un concert de présentation.

items.title: Afrique du Sud: des femmes en colère manifestent pour réclamer justice face aux féminicides

original_payload.original_title: Afrique du Sud: des femmes en colère manifestent pour réclamer justice face aux féminicides
original_payload.original_body:
Afrique du Sud: des femmes en colère manifestent pour réclamer justice face aux féminicides
Il y a un an, à la veille du lancement du G20 en Afrique du Sud, des milliers de femmes participaient à un sit-in silencieux à travers le pays pour dénoncer les féminicides dont les taux sont parmi les plus élevés au monde. Les manifestantes avaient alors obtenu que ces violences soient classées comme catastrophe nationale. Un an plus tard, jour pour jour, elles sont de nouveau dans la rue, ce samedi 21 novembre, pour dénoncer une situation toujours dramatique et réclamer davantage de moyens concrets.
Publié le :  21/11/2026 - 14:31
A travers les rues de Johannesburg, en Afrique du Sud, quelques centaines de personnes suivent un cercueil noir et violet. Il symbolise les femmes victimes de féminicides, une manifestation pour dénoncer une situation toujours dramatique et réclamer davantage de moyens concrets, le 21 novembre 2026.        AFP - ILARIA FINIZIO
Par :
RFI
Avec notre correspondante à Johannesburg,   Joséphine Kloeckner
À travers les rues de Johannesburg, quelques centaines de personnes suivent un cercueil noir et violet. Il symbolise les femmes victimes de féminicides.
Dans le cortège, des survivantes et des familles de victimes qui, pour beaucoup, attendent toujours que justice soit rendue. Après 15 minutes de silence, pour 15 femmes tuées chaque jour dans le pays, la ministre des Femmes, de la jeunesse et des personnes en situation de handicap est venue, en personne, recevoir une lettre de demandes de l’organisation Women for Change.
Toujours pas d'objectifs ni d'actions tangibles
Son discours - dans lequel elle assure l’implication du gouvernement dans la lutte contre les violences de genre - est vite étouffé sous les huées des femmes en colère qui réclament de passer de la parole aux actes. La foule s’empare du micro, de nombreuses femmes racontent, en larmes, les violences dont elles ont été victimes et les proches qu’elles ont perdu.
Un an après la classification des violences de genre comme catastrophe nationale, le plan d’action du gouvernement ne présente toujours pas d’objectifs chiffrés, ni d’actions tangibles, malgré l’annonce de fonds supplémentaires, il y a un mois.

items.title: Firm Blames Anambra Power Crisis On National Grid, Says It Received About 107mw Despite 1000mw Demand

original_payload.original_title: Firm Blames Anambra Power Crisis On National Grid, Says It Received About 107mw Despite 1000mw Demand
original_payload.original_body:
The FirstPower Electricity Distribution Company Limited has blamed the worsening electricity supply across Anambra State on declining national grid generation and inadequate power allocation.
The company said that its network received less than 107 megawatts (MW) on every day of the past week, despite the state requiring about 1,000MW to meet its energy needs.
The electricity distribution company made this known in a statement issued on Friday, November 20, 2026, by its Head of Communications, Izunna Okafor, amid growing concerns among residents, businesses and industries over persistent power shortages and inconsistent electricity supply across the state.
The company said the situation was part of wider challenges confronting Nigeria's electricity sector, particularly fluctuations in power generation and reduced allocations from the national grid to the country's 11 electricity distribution companies (DisCos).
“Recent reports and data from the Nigerian Independent System Operator (NISO) show that electricity generation has been fluctuating considerably, with a noticeable decline in the volume of energy available for distribution to the country's 11 electricity distribution companies (DisCos),” Okafor stated.
“Yesterday, November 19, 2026, national grid generation was reported to have dropped from 3,743 megawatts (MW) around midnight to 3,179MW by 6 a.m., and later increasing marginally to 3,180MW by 6 p.m.
“The development left the 11 distribution companies with a total allocation of approximately 2,885MW to be shared among themselves, further constraining electricity supply across the country.”
Okafor added, “In that allocation of 2,885MW, Abuja DisCo received the highest allocation of 551MW, followed by Ikeja DisCo with 366MW, Ibadan DisCo with 340MW, and Eko DisCo with 339MW.
“Port Harcourt DisCo received 279MW, Benin DisCo 230MW, EEDC (which FirstPower operates under) got 220MW, Kano DisCo 173MW, Kaduna DisCo 167MW, and Jos DisCo 146MW, while Yola DisCo got 74MW. This shows the level of general drop in supply across the country, as a result of the drop in generation.
“Down here at the level of FirstPower's distribution network in Anambra State, the situation is reflected in the combined electricity allocation received through the four TCN interface stations serving the company: Awada, GCM, Nibo and Agu-Awka.”
The company said that its operational records showed that the network received 90.52MW on November 13, increasing to 95.50MW on November 14 and 106.73MW on November 15.
However, according to the company, the allocation subsequently crashed to 64.34MW on November 16 before rising to 80.13MW on November 17 and 81.37MW on November 18.
It further declined slightly to 80.55MW on November 19 before recovering to 91.33MW as of 7:16am on Friday.
FirstPower acknowledged that although the latest allocation represented an improvement over the previous day, it remained significantly below the 106.73MW received on November 15.
The company said the fluctuations had made it difficult to maintain consistent electricity supply across Anambra State.
The admission comes against the backdrop of Governor Chukwuma Soludo's disclosure at a recent investment roundtable organised by the Anambra State Electricity Regulatory Commission (ASERC) that the state requires approximately 1,000MW of electricity but currently receives only about 120MW at most.
FirstPower's latest figures indicate that its distribution network has not received up to 107MW on any single day within the reviewed week, further highlighting the gap between the state's electricity requirements and the power currently available to consumers.
In a bid to address the shortfall, FirstPower said that it recently signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Greenewable Energy Limited for the development of 100MW of embedded electricity generation in Anambra State.
The agreement, the company said, was signed during the investment roundtable organised by ASERC, with FirstPower describing the proposed project as part of efforts to diversify its energy sources and increase electricity availability for residents.
The company, however, did not provide a specific timeline for the commencement or completion of the proposed 100MW project.
FirstPower also sought to clarify its position within the electricity value chain, stressing that it does not generate the electricity it distributes to consumers.
The company likened its operations to those of a distributor who cannot supply goods beyond the quantity received from a manufacturer.
While acknowledging the difficulties faced by households, businesses and industries, FirstPower appealed to residents to exercise patience and understanding, particularly as economic and commercial activities increase ahead of the festive season.
It assured customers that it would continue working with EEDC, TCN, NISO and other relevant stakeholders to improve electricity allocation and stabilise supply across its distribution network.
The company also promised to manage available electricity more efficiently and equitably while monitoring developments in the national power sector.

items.title: Indian National Sentenced To Nearly 20 Years In US For Plotting To Assassinate Sikh Leader

original_payload.original_title: Indian National Sentenced To Nearly 20 Years In US For Plotting To Assassinate Sikh Leader
original_payload.original_body:
A 55-year-old Indian national, Nikhil Gupta, has been sentenced to 235 months (nearly 20 years) in a United States prison for his role in a plot allegedly orchestrated by an Indian government employee to assassinate Sikh separatist leader and US-based attorney Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York City.
Gupta was sentenced on Friday by US District Judge Victor Marrero in the Southern District of New York after pleading guilty in February 2026 to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering.
The US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York announced the sentence, describing the case as an assassination conspiracy allegedly directed by an employee of the Indian government.
According to the US Justice Department, Gupta worked with Vikash Yadav, an alleged Indian government employee, to arrange Pannun's murder on American soil in 2023.
Yadav was identified in court documents as an employee of India's Cabinet Secretariat, which houses the country's foreign intelligence agency, the Research and Analysis Wing (RAW).
Prosecutors said Yadav recruited Gupta in May 2023 to organise the killing of Pannun, a US citizen of Indian origin who leads a US-based organisation advocating for the independence of Punjab, a northern Indian state with a large Sikh population.
Pannun has been an outspoken critic of the Indian government and has advocated for the establishment of an independent Sikh state known as Khalistan. The Indian government has banned him and his separatist organisation from operating in India.
The court documents revealed that Gupta approached an individual he believed to be a criminal associate to help recruit a contract killer.
However, the individual was actually a confidential source working with the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), who subsequently introduced Gupta to an undercover DEA officer posing as a hitman.
Prosecutors said Yadav, through arrangements brokered by Gupta, agreed to pay the undercover officer $100,000 to assassinate Pannun.
On June 9, 2023, Gupta and Yadav allegedly arranged for an associate to deliver $15,000 in cash to the undercover officer as an advance payment for the killing.
The US Justice Department further disclosed that Yadav supplied Gupta with sensitive personal information about Pannun, including his residential address in New York, telephone numbers and details of his daily movements.
Gupta subsequently passed the information to the undercover officer and regularly updated Yadav on the operation, including providing surveillance photographs of the intended victim.
Investigators said Gupta repeatedly instructed the undercover officer to carry out the assassination as quickly as possible but warned him not to execute the operation around the time Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi was scheduled to visit the United States on an official state visit beginning June 20, 2023.
The plot reportedly took a more urgent turn following the killing of another prominent Sikh separatist leader, Hardeep Singh Nijjar, in Canada.
On June 18, 2023, masked gunmen shot Nijjar dead outside a Sikh temple in British Columbia, Canada.
Nijjar, like Pannun, was a prominent advocate of the Khalistan movement and a vocal critic of the Indian government.
According to prosecutors, Gupta contacted the undercover officer on June 19, the day after Nijjar's killing, and disclosed that Nijjar had also been a target.
He reportedly told the undercover officer that there were "so many targets" and that, following Nijjar's killing, there was "now no need to wait" before carrying out the assassination of Pannun.
Gupta was arrested in the Czech Republic on June 30, 2023, at the request of US authorities and was subsequently extradited to the United States in June 2024.
Announcing the sentence, US Attorney Jamie McDonald said the punishment reflected the seriousness of Gupta's actions and warned that American authorities would pursue individuals involved in planning violence against US citizens, regardless of where they operated.
"While in India, Gupta helped to methodically plan the victim's murder, believing he was beyond the reach of a U.S. court. But Gupta was wrong," McDonald said.
He added that the sentence demonstrated the US government's commitment to prosecuting individuals involved in violent plots on American soil.
Gupta was also ordered to pay a $300 special assessment in addition to his prison sentence.

items.title: Tinubu Appoints Ex-Lagos Commissioner Dabiri To NASS Service Commission

original_payload.original_title: Tinubu Appoints Ex-Lagos Commissioner Dabiri To NASS Service Commission
original_payload.original_body:
President Bola Tinubu has approved the appointment of former Lagos State Commissioner for Youth and Social Development, Agboola Lukman Dabiri, as the South-West representative on the National Assembly Service Commission (NASC).
Dabiri replaces Taiwo Olukemi Oluwa, who resigned from the commission on March 30, 2026, to contest the 2027 general election for the Irewole/Isokan Federal Constituency in Osun State.
The appointment was announced on Friday in a statement issued by the President’s Special Adviser on Information and Strategy, Bayo Onanuga.
According to the statement, Dabiri previously served as Commissioner for Youth and Social Development in Lagos State.
He also served as Mandate Secretary for Economic Planning, Revenue Generation and Public-Private Partnership in the Federal Capital Territory.
Onanuga said the appointment was part of Tinubu’s efforts to ensure effective representation and inclusivity in the National Assembly Service Commission.
“The appointment is part of the President’s efforts to ensure effective representation and inclusivity in the National Assembly Service Commission,” the statement read.
The National Assembly Service Commission is responsible for the appointment, promotion and discipline of staff of the National Assembly.
Established under Section 157 of the 1999 Constitution, the commission plays a key role in overseeing the administration and personnel management of the National Assembly.
Dabiri’s appointment fills the South-West position previously occupied by Oluwa, who stepped down to pursue her political ambition ahead of the 2027 general elections.
The development comes as political activities gather momentum ahead of the 2027 polls, with several public office holders and political actors positioning themselves for elective offices.
