items.title: Burundi: l'opposant Agathon Rwasa a déposé sa candidature à la présidentielle de 2027

original_payload.original_title: Burundi: l'opposant Agathon Rwasa a déposé sa candidature à la présidentielle de 2027
original_payload.original_body:
Burundi: l'opposant Agathon Rwasa a déposé sa candidature à la présidentielle de 2027
Au Burundi, c’est ce dimanche que s’achève la période de dépôt des candidatures pour l’élection présidentielle du 3 mai 2027. Après le président Évariste Ndayishimiye qui brigue un second mandat de 7 ans et quelques candidats peu connus du grand public, l’opposant et ancien premier vice-président de l’Assemblée nationale Agathon Rwasa, arrivé deuxième à la présidentielle de 2020, a déposé samedi son dossier. Privé de son parti et face à la machine du CNDD-FDD qui dirige depuis plus de 20 ans le pays, il estime malgré tout qu’il est de son devoir de concourir malgré les menaces qui pèsent sur sa candidature.
Publié le :  22/11/2026 - 06:15
2 min     Temps de lecture
Agathon Rwasa parle à la presse à Bujumbura, le 28 mai 2020.        AFP - -
Par :
RFI
Publicité
Envers et contre tous Agathon Rwasa, a déposé sa candidature à l’élection présidentielle en tant qu’indépendant, puisqu'il a été évincé de la tête de son parti au profit d’un proche du pouvoir en 2024.
À lire aussi  Burundi: l'opposition suspend sa participation à l'élection présidentielle de 2027
L’année suivante, la Commission électorale avait écarté sa candidature aux législatives pour ce motif, mais «  les deux années prévues par la loi désormais sont révolues  », affirme l’ancien chef rebelle, bien que ses détracteurs estiment qu'en saisissant la Cour suprême pour contester son éviction il se revendique encore du CNL, ce qui n’est pas compatible avec une candidature indépendante.
«  J'aurais été coupable si je m'abstenais  »
Plusieurs partis boycottent le scrutin, mais «  j'aurais été coupable si je m'abstenais  », dit au contraire Agathon Rwasa qui veut «  offrir une alternative  » pour « ne pas laisser le terrain libre au CNDD-FDD » depuis plus de 20 ans au pouvoir, qui contrôle déjà la totalité des sièges à l’Assemblée nationale, ainsi que les institutions d’un pays en proie aux pénuries et à l’inflation. « J'ai un idéal à défendre », martèle Agathon Rwasa.
Fin septembre, Fortuné Gaetan Zongo, rapporteur spécial des Nations unies sur la situation des droits de l'homme au   Burundi  , alertait sur plusieurs signaux susceptibles de compromettre la tenue d'élections présidentielles libres et crédibles en 2027, soulignant notamment les restrictions au pluralisme, la fermeture de l'espace civique et médiatique et les violations des droits humains. «  Une élection ne peut être libre si les principaux concurrents sont exclus  », avait il déclaré.
Quant à la commission électorale, elle dispose de quatre jours pour analyser les dossiers et donnera sa réponse le 27 novembre prochain. Après l’examen d’éventuels recours, la liste définitive des candidats à l’élection présidentielle est attendue pour le 6 décembre.
Si la Céni joue franc et respecte les dispositions légales en vigueur, il n'y pas lieu qu'elle rejette ma candidature.

items.title: Le Gabon augmente ses capacités de production d'électricité avec un nouveau barrage hydroélectrique

original_payload.original_title: Le Gabon augmente ses capacités de production d'électricité avec un nouveau barrage hydroélectrique
original_payload.original_body:
Le Gabon augmente ses capacités de production d'électricité avec un nouveau barrage hydroélectrique
Au Gabon, plusieurs quartiers de Libreville seront plongés dans le noir pendant trois jours successifs du 27 au 29 novembre prochain, a prévenu le gouvernement. Il ne s’agira pas d’une panne mais des travaux de maintenance d’un pipeline qui achemine le gaz de Port-Gentil à Libreville. Bonne nouvelle dans le même temps, le ministre de l'Énergie Olivier Mouckocko a annoncé la fin des travaux du nouveau barrage hydroélectrique de Kinguelé aval.
Publié le :  22/11/2026 - 05:50
1 min     Temps de lecture
Vue générale du quartier administratif de Libreville, Gabon, le 7 septembre 2023.        AFP - -
Par :
RFI
Publicité
Avec notre correspondant à Libreville,   Yves-Laurent Goma
Le nouveau barrage est appelé Kinguelé aval parce qu’il a été construit en aval d’une rivière sur laquelle deux autres barrages existent déjà. Il s’agit de celui de Kinguelé et de Tchimbelé dont la production cumulée est de 120 MW.
Kinguelé aval produira 35 MW soit près de 13 % des besoins en électricité de Libreville et ses environs. L’investissement réalisé en partenariat public-privé a coûté 120 milliards de FCFA, soit environ 183 millions d'euros, pour des travaux qui ont duré 5 ans.
Malgré ce nouveau barrage, le   Gabon   ne pourra pas si tôt rompre son contrat avec la société turque Karpowership. Celle-ci a mis à disposition   deux bateaux usines qui produisent 150 MW d’électricité   sans réellement satisfaire une demande en très nette augmentation.
En effet, la création, depuis plusieurs décennies, de nombreuses industries, notamment dans le secteur du bois, a explosé la demande en énergie alors que sa production n'a pas suivi, les centrales ayant également vieilli, d’où les nombreux délestages constatés dans la capitale.

Babatunde Olofin, the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of Moniepoint Microfinance Bank says transaction volume of the bank has hit one trillion naira daily.

”From the very beginning, we built this distribution network of people that can be trusted, I think this is just an extension of our hyper-local strategy, getting closer to people,” she said.

items.title: Firm seeks stronger data protection through international e-waste standards

original_payload.original_title: Firm seeks stronger data protection through international e-waste standards
original_payload.original_body:
Science & Tech  Firm seeks stronger data protection through international e-waste standards
By  Ndubisi Ijeoma   ·   2 hours ago   ·  3 min read
✓
✓
By Deborah Abodurin and Stellamaris Ashinze
E-Terra Technologies Ltd. has called for stronger adoption of international standards in electronic waste recycling and secure data destruction to prevent data breaches.
The Managing Director, Ifeanyi Ochonogor, made the call on Friday in Lagos ahead of the Data Destruction Exposition 2026.
Ochonogor warned that improper disposal of electronic devices and storage equipment could expose individuals, businesses and government institutions to security breaches.
He said obsolete electronic equipment required responsible disposal to protect confidential information and prevent environmental pollution.
The E-Terra chief executive disclosed that the company had obtained three International Organisation for Standardisation (ISO) certifications covering its operational processes.
According to him, the certifications ensure that its electronic waste recycling and data destruction activities comply with internationally recognised standards.
He said the forthcoming exposition would promote responsible data disposal, encourage industry best practices and address Nigeria’s growing electronic waste challenges.
“There is need for stronger government support and competition to strengthen Nigeria’s electronic waste recycling and data destruction industry,” he said.
Ochonogor described data destruction as an established industry in developed countries, urging greater attention to its development in Nigeria.
He said the company’s operations covered different categories of electronic waste, including cathode ray tube (CRT) equipment.
He stressed that environmental protection remained central to the company’s recycling processes and technological operations.
Ochonogor also disclosed that E-Terra was working towards developing electronic waste refining capacity through its affiliated organisations.
He identified confidential information protection, obsolete information technology asset management and responsible recycling as critical to Nigeria’s digital future.
He said the company regularly reviewed and upgraded its processes to address emerging environmental challenges and technological developments, including artificial intelligence.
According to him, E-Terra’s operations involved engagement with relevant government institutions, including the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) and Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC).
He added that the company supported electronic waste awareness and capacity-building programmes, particularly among students and electronic waste handlers.
Ochonogor said the E-Waste Relief Foundation had organised school awareness campaigns and training initiatives for electronic waste handlers.
He expressed hope that the exposition would become an annual event, providing a platform for stronger collaboration among industry stakeholders.
The Data Destruction Exposition 2026 is scheduled for Nov. 26 in Lagos, bringing together government institutions, regulatory agencies, technology companies, data protection professionals and environmental experts.
With the theme around data destruction and confidential information protection, the event aims to strengthen data security and promote environmentally responsible electronic waste management. (NAN)
Edited by Kamal Tayo Oropo

original_payload.original_title: Fossil fuel impasse pushes COP31 climate talks into second day of overtime
original_payload.original_body:
Turkish officials have asked negotiators at the COP31 climate summit to consider a last-minute proposal as talks stretched into a second  day of overtime  over the fossil fuels issue.
“We believe that we have put forward a text which all the parties can agree upon,” COP31 President Murat Kurum told a late-night plenary session on Saturday.
Recommended Stories

list 2 of 3  COP31 deal stalls as nations struggle to agree on climate plan
list 3 of 3  Gen Z protests sweep Europe over wars, rising costs and climate

Kurum, who is also Turkiye’s environment minister, said the conference would reconvene later on Sunday morning to approve the deal.
The latest text was not immediately made public, and it was unclear if negotiators had received the wording overnight, which would give nations only a few hours to submit objections and changes.
An earlier draft had drawn strong condemnation for failing to mention fossil fuels, the largest contributors to climate change.
Kurum said he ⁠believed concerns around fossil fuels had ‌been addressed, as had those ‌around helping developing countries finance their adaptations to climate change.
The new ‌text followed intensive consultations between Australia, which is ‌leading the talks; Turkiye, which is hosting the meeting; and nearly 200 delegations from many of the world’s richest, poorest, largest and smallest nations.
Delegations had until 03:00 GMT on Sunday to ‌raise any objections to the deal, with a session scheduled at 06:00 GMT to ⁠begin approving ⁠it.
The summit’s agreement is meant to address how the world will deal with climate change, which drives heatwaves, floods and other disasters.

items.title: Eleven killed in burst of violence during Mexican cartel leader’s capture

original_payload.original_title: Eleven killed in burst of violence during Mexican cartel leader’s capture
original_payload.original_body:
The operation to capture Mexican cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores in the country’s Sinaloa state has left at least 11 people dead.
Mexico’s Defence Ministry said on Saturday that seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed in the overnight operation.

list 2 of 3  Migrant caravan sets out from southern Mexico bound for US after midterms
list 3 of 3  Founder of Guadalajara cartel dies in hospital after decades in prison

Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro”, was  captured on Friday  and flown to Mexico City on Saturday after hours-long violence involving a firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen overnight, roadblocks and burning trucks in the city of Guasave.
Two other men were also captured and flown to Mexico City. The ministry identified them as German N, known as “Serafin”, the group’s alleged second-in-command, and Jose N, an alleged financial operator of the cartel. Both were also flown to Mexico City and handed over to prosecutors.
Meza Flores, one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives, climbed the ranks to lead the Beltrán Leyva cartel and later became the boss of his own group, the Meza-Flores transnational criminal organisation.
He was also a key ally to “Los Mayos”, a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which the United States designated as a “foreign terrorist organization” last year.
The US wanted Meza Flores for trafficking drugs to the country and offered a $5m reward for information leading to his arrest.
A poster from the FBI’s Most Wanted Fugitive list shows an undated photo of Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, also known as ‘Chapo Isidro’ [AFP]   Residents terrified
The firefight in Guasave broke out about 7pm on Friday (02:00 GMT on Saturday), according to residents. Military helicopters and drones were soon flying overhead, with helicopters opening fire on key locations across the city.

items.title: Overturned boat carrying mourners to funeral kills at least 24 in Nigeria

original_payload.original_title: Overturned boat carrying mourners to funeral kills at least 24 in Nigeria
original_payload.original_body:
A boat believed to be carrying hundreds of attendees to a funeral has overturned in southern Nigeria, killing at least 24 people, according to authorities.
The overcrowded vessel capsized on Friday in Bayelsa State after a mechanical failure while travelling from the communities of Ayama to Ukubie, according to police.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items    list 1 of 3  Nigeria launches hunt for hundreds of kidnapped mosque worshippers
list 2 of 3  Niger’s military-led government says it contained mutiny: What next?
list 3 of 3  More than 80 reported abducted in Nigeria as police find human remains
end of list
“So far, 24 bodies have been recovered from the scene of the incident, while search and rescue operations are ongoing,” Manzo Ezekiel, a spokesman for the National Emergency Management Agency, said on Saturday.
Rescue and search operations were continuing, he added.
Two children were among the four bodies initially recovered from the water on Friday, police said at the time, adding that 24 people were rescued, with 19 treated at a local clinic and five taken to hospital in the state capital.
Police did not say how many people were on board, but some residents told the Reuters news agency there were at least 300.
Police said the driver fled and the vessel’s manager was taken into custody.
According to a statement from the Bayelsa State Police Command, the accident occurred at the river junction between the Oweikorogha and Otuan communities, in the state’s Southern Ijaw district.
The boat that capsized was travelling “for a burial ceremony”, the statement also said, adding that police are “coordinating efforts with local divers and other responders”.
Such boat accidents are common on Nigeria’s busy rivers and waterways, often caused by overloaded vessels, poor maintenance, or failure to comply with safety regulations.

items.title: Displaced Palestinians protest as Israeli air strikes continue in Gaza

original_payload.original_title: Displaced Palestinians protest as Israeli air strikes continue in Gaza
original_payload.original_body:
Hundreds of displaced Palestinians have protested as Israeli forces continue to destroy residential buildings in Gaza, beyond the line they withdrew to under last year’s ceasefire.
Al Jazeera journalist Moath al-Kahlout, reporting from Gaza’s Deir el-Balah, said displaced Palestinians who live in the area near the “Yellow Line” gathered on Saturday to demonstrate against Israel’s intensifying air strikes.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items    list 1 of 3  Demolition notices for buildings in Hebron provoke fear among Palestinians
list 2 of 3  Israeli strike on vehicle distributing food aid in Gaza kills three
list 3 of 3  Jerusalem Daily: Gaza faces deadly strikes and health crisis

The “ Yellow Line”  separates Israeli- and Hamas-controlled areas in Gaza since the “ceasefire” signed in October 2025.
“More than 500 housing units have been destroyed in less than a month,” said Mohammed Musleh, mayor of Deir-el Balah’s Maghazi municipality, told Al Jazeera.
“This is part of what appears to be a systematic policy of gradual creeping displacement aimed at forcing residents out of their camp and destroying as many homes as possible,” Musleh said.
Gaza’s Ministry of Public Works and Housing says 350,000 families are homeless after Israeli attacks destroyed 80 percent of the enclave’s homes.
Meanwhile, flooding in recent weeks  devastated temporary tent housing , the ministry said.
The original “Yellow Line”, established under US President Donald Trump’s 20-point plan to end Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, marked the area to which Israeli forces initially withdrew. They were expected to make further withdrawals gradually, but instead seized more territory.
“If we go back to October 2025, when the ceasefire was signed, the ‘Yellow Line’ was much further east,” al-Kahlout said.

items.title: Displaced Darfur families face volatile winter as Sudan aid cuts bite

original_payload.original_title: Displaced Darfur families face volatile winter as Sudan aid cuts bite
original_payload.original_body:
Omdurman, Sudan –  When Fatima Mohamed Haroun was displaced from West Darfur state at the start of Sudan’s war in 2023, she never imagined she would find herself caring for four of her grandchildren far from her home.
Haroun, who believes she is aged about 60, said her son went missing a year ago. His wife died after giving birth, leaving Haroun as the sole guardian of her four grandchildren.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items    list 1 of 3  Sudan’s war leaves disabled children missing out on education
list 2 of 3  Sudan’s war will end, but will it be too late?
list 3 of 3  Sudan’s elderly face hardship and heartbreak in a life of displacement
end of list
Now living in a crumbling mudbrick building in al-Ghadir, north of Omdurman, in Khartoum state, she has received no humanitarian assistance since her displacement.
Without an income, it is only the goodwill of her neighbours that prevents Haroun and her grandchildren from starving. But every day is a battle to find food, water or medicine, and with winter fast approaching, proper shelter, warm clothes, and blankets for the children are another priority.
“I cannot work or earn money, so we depend on neighbours who occasionally give us food. But even our neighbours sometimes have nothing to eat. When they have no food, my grandchildren and I go to bed hungry,” she told Al Jazeera.
“We have no supplies to help us cope with the cold, not even blankets to keep us warm. We sleep on the ground with only the sky above us. The cold is severe, and the children are suffering. We appeal to the government and humanitarian organisations to provide food, blankets, covers and other basic necessities to help us endure the cold and protect our children.”
Fatima Mohamed Haroun, a displaced woman from Darfur supporting her four grandchildren, in the al-Ghadir area, north of Omdurman [Abdelazim Allahgabo/Al Jazeera]   Temperatures can drop significantly in Omdurman during the winter, and at night al-Ghadir can be particularly cold due to its location close to mountainous areas. Displaced families living in temporary shelters here are especially vulnerable because they lack blankets, winter clothing and heating facilities.

items.title: South Korea education minister resigns over AI cheating scandal

original_payload.original_title: South Korea education minister resigns over AI cheating scandal
original_payload.original_body:
South Korea’s education minister resigned Sunday over an AI-assisted cheating scandal that erupted ahead of the country’s key college entrance exams last week.
The country has been gripped by fears of AI-assisted exam cheating since last Sunday, when the top scorer in a national tax accountant exam confessed to using a miniature camera and smartphone to achieve a near-perfect score, just four days before the crucial college entrance exam known as the Suneung.
The annual nine-hour Suneung is widely seen as a ticket to prestigious universities, well-paid jobs and even better marriage prospects in the highly competitive country.
The confession sent officials scrambling to roll out a slew of preventive measures — including blocking public Wi-Fi in testing areas and placing stickers over clothing buttons but Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin struggled to reassure the public, particularly after remarks he made three days before the exam.

items.title: FULL LIST: FG announces 19 international job vacancies

original_payload.original_title: FULL LIST: FG announces 19 international job vacancies
original_payload.original_body:
The Federal Government has announced 19 vacancies for Nigerians at the African Space Agency and the General Secretariat of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, with application deadlines running from November 25 to December 24, 2026.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs disclosed this in two separate vacancy announcements dated Friday, November 20, 2026, which were signed by the ministry’s spokesperson, Oluwafemi Adeniyi, and shared on its official Facebook page on Saturday.
In the announcement on the African Space Agency, the ministry said the organisation was recruiting for five positions at its headquarters in Cairo, Egypt.
It stated that “interested and qualified Nigerians are encouraged to visit the official website of the Agency at  https://africanspaceagency.org  for more information on eligibility criteria and application procedures.”

SOMMAIRE
La Roma à quatre points en Ligue des champions
Le Paris Saint-Germain retrouvera mercredi une Roma portée par un attaquant en pleine réussite. Donyell Malen a marqué quatre fois samedi 21 novembre lors de la victoire du club italien sur la pelouse de Parme (5-1), à quatre jours de leur rencontre de la cinquième journée de Ligue des champions au Parc des Princes.
L’international néerlandais a ouvert le score à la 39e minute. Parme est revenu à hauteur au retour des vestiaires grâce à Nesta Elphege, mais Malen a redonné l’avantage aux Romains à la 68e minute. Rodrigo Mora a ensuite inscrit le troisième but, avant que Malen ne marque de nouveau à la 77e et à la 90e minute. L’attaquant totalise désormais 12 buts en 11 matches de Serie A cette saison, selon les chiffres publiés par l’AS Roma.
Après cette victoire, l’entraîneur Gian Piero Gasperini a mis en avant, au micro de DAZN, le rôle donné à Malen dans l’animation offensive et la manière dont ses qualités s’accordent avec celles de ses coéquipiers. La Roma compte désormais 30 points en championnat et occupe la deuxième place.
La Roma à quatre points en Ligue des champions
Le rendez-vous européen s’annonce plus difficile pour les Italiens. Après quatre journées, la Roma compte quatre points grâce à un nul contre Fenerbahçe (1-1) et une victoire sur le Slovan Bratislava (4-0). Elle s’est inclinée face au Real Madrid (3-4), puis à Manchester United (2-3). Le PSG, lui, a remporté ses quatre premières rencontres et affiche douze points, avec vingt buts inscrits, selon les résultats officiels de l’UEFA.
PSG–Roma se jouera mercredi 25 novembre à 21 heures, heure de Cotonou. Paris abordera cette rencontre après sa victoire à Nice (3-2), marquée par  la blessure au genou de Désiré Doué , sorti sur civière samedi. L’équipe de Luis Enrique doit encore préciser la durée de son indisponibilité.

items.title: CAF endorses Infantino for re-election as FIFA president

original_payload.original_title: CAF endorses Infantino for re-election as FIFA president
original_payload.original_body:
Soccer Football – 48th CAF Ordinary General Assembly – Bola Ahmed Tinubu International Conference Centre, Abuja, Nigeria – November 21, 2026 FIFA president Gianni Infantino with CAF president Patrice Motsepe, vice president Fouzi Lekjaa and members during the general assembly [File photo: Reuters/Marvellous Durowaiye] Confederation of African Football (CAF) president Patrice Motsepe has again endorsed Gianni Infantino for re-election as FIFA President as the Swiss confirmed a huge increase in grant payments ​to each member association on Saturday.
Speaking at the organisation’s Ordinary General Assembly ‌in Abuja, Nigeria, Motsepe said CAF was backing Infantino for another term following challenges from French Football Federation president Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima, honorary president of the Japan Football Association.
“I have experienced ​over the last five years (as CAF president) his deep commitment. Gianni, you have ​our support among the 54 member associations of CAF,” Motsepe said.
Infantino ⁠said he would continue to put developing football in Africa at the forefront of ​his agenda while FIFA president.
“You will always find in me and in FIFA a trusted ​partner, a trusted brother, to make sure that the dreams that we all have, the dreams that these children have in Abuja, in Cape Town, in Cairo, everywhere in Africa, can become reality,” ​he said.
Infantino reiterated the plan to more than triple the grant given to FIFA ​member associations around the world, from the current $8 million over a four-year period to $25 million.
It will be ‌effective ⁠from January 2027, three months before the FIFA presidential elections in Morocco.
The plan to increase the grants under the new FIFA Forward 4.0 programme had been mooted in October, and is set to be ratified at a FIFA Council meeting next month.
“When I was ​first elected (in 2016), each ​federation was receiving ⁠from FIFA $250,000 a year, or $1 million every four years for football development,” Infantino said.
“Now, 10 years later, you will receive $25 million to ​invest in football development. And we will work to make ​it even ⁠more than that. Because you deserve it. Because your youth deserve it.
“FIFA’s money is your money, and you invest it in infrastructure, in development and in opportunities.
“We believe in Africa, because ⁠we ​love Africa, because we are Africa,” he said to ​rapturous applause.
CONMEBOL on Friday reaffirmed its unanimous support for Infantino’s bid for another term, with all 10 member associations ​of the South American confederation backing his candidacy.
Source:  Reuters

items.title: NATO will defend every inch of Polish territory, Rutte says

original_payload.original_title: NATO will defend every inch of Polish territory, Rutte says
original_payload.original_body:
FILE – NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte speaks to the media on the day of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group meeting at NATO headquarters in Brussels, Belgium, November 17, 2026. [File photo: Reuters/Stephanie Lecocq] NATO will defend every inch of Polish territory, NATO Secretary General ​Mark Rutte said in Warsaw, a day after Poland ‌said Russia violated its airspace with three objects that were probably two missiles and a drone.
“I can guarantee that NATO will defend every ​inch of Polish territory,” Rutte said, Polish Press Agency ​PAP reported on Saturday.
The head of NATO forces in ⁠Europe, General Alexus Grynkewich, would do everything necessary to ​identify any threats to defense and deterrence capabilities and would ​implement appropriate adjustments if needed, Rutte said, according to PAP.
Drones have repeatedly strayed into the airspace of countries on NATO’s eastern flank during Russia’s ​war in Ukraine, fuelling tension with the Western military ​alliance and stoking fears that the conflict could spread.
Friday’s intrusion came as ‌Poland ⁠was hosting military exercises involving the “Coalition of the Willing” that groups allies of Ukraine, a coincidence Polish officials described as not accidental.
On Monday, a meeting of NATO’s North Atlantic Council ​will be held ​in Brussels ⁠to discuss the violation of Polish airspace by Russian missiles, PAP also reported on Saturday.
“In the ​near future, we will receive strong support ​from our ⁠NATO allies to bolster the protection of our eastern border,” Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote on X on Saturday, commenting ⁠on the ​meeting of the NATO body.
“I’ve been ​in contact today with general Grynkewich, to coordinate the details of these measures.”
Source:  Reuters

items.title: Thousands march in Lisbon as living costs fuel anger

original_payload.original_title: Thousands march in Lisbon as living costs fuel anger
original_payload.original_body:
] People shout slogans during a CGTP trade union protest demanding higher wages, increase in pensions and against the rising cost of living, in Lisbon, Portugal, November 21, 2026. [Photo: Reuters/Pedro Nunes] Thousands of people marched through central Lisbon on Saturday despite heavy rain to protest against soaring ​living costs, a deepening housing crisis and low wages.
Organiser CGTP, ‌Portugal’s largest trade union federation, called for higher wages and pensions, lower prices for essential goods and services, and measures to curb housing costs.
The CGTP said ​turnout reached “many thousands” as protesters carrying umbrellas and wearing hooded ponchos ​marched along two of Lisbon’s main avenues. Police did not ⁠provide an estimate.
“We work more, we have more expenses and we ​don’t have money for day-to-day life,” said Manuel Gomes, 44, a factory ​worker, arguing that the centre-right government’s policies had made matters worse..
“Our wages are low, diesel and gasoline prices keep going up, and so do housing costs and ​everything else. We have to change this,” Gomes said.
Portugal’s average annual earnings ​in 2025 were 37% below the European Union average, according to Eurostat. Inflation hit 3.8% ‌in ⁠October, driven by food and energy prices amid continuing tensions in the Middle East.
Portugal is also grappling with one of Europe’s most severe housing affordability crises. House prices have more than doubled since 2017, while rents ​for new leases have ​nearly doubled, ⁠hitting younger people particularly hard.
Luis Russo, 66, a retired IT technician, said he was demonstrating to demand “higher wages ​and pensions and against speculation in the rental market”, ​accusing the ⁠government of serving “big interests” rather than ordinary people.
The protest followed weeks of unrest, including housing activists’ tent camps in Lisbon and Porto, and comes amid ⁠a broader ​wave of demonstrations across Europe over living ​costs and housing. Turnout at largely peaceful protests in France on Saturday was lower than in ​previous weeks.
Source:  Reuters

items.title: South Africa’s first female deputy president and UN official dies

original_payload.original_title: South Africa’s first female deputy president and UN official dies
original_payload.original_body:
Executive Director of UN Women Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka attends the Women's Forum Americas, at Claustro de Sor Juana University in Mexico City, Mexico, May 30, 2019. [Photo: Reuters/Henry Romero] South Africa’s first female deputy president, Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, ​who also served as UN ‌under-secretary-general and executive director of UN Women, has died at the age of ​71, the presidency said late ​on Friday.
Elected as a member of ⁠parliament in 1994 in South ​Africa’s first democratic government, former teacher ​Mlambo-Ngcuka served as deputy president of South Africa from 2005 to 2008.
Before becoming deputy ​president, a role in which ​she oversaw government initiatives to reduce poverty ‌with ⁠a focus on women, Mlambo-Ngcuka served as the minister of minerals and energy and as a deputy ​minister in ​the ⁠Department of Trade and Industry.
In August 2013 she took ​the oath of office as ​executive ⁠director of UN Women, serving two terms at an organization created ⁠to ​lead the UN’s work ​on advancing gender equality and women’s empowerment
Source:  Reuters

items.title: Kenya’s internet metering bill raises privacy and affordability concerns

original_payload.original_title: Kenya’s internet metering bill raises privacy and affordability concerns
original_payload.original_body:
Nairobi, Kenya –  A proposed law requiring internet service providers in Kenya to monitor subscribers’ data consumption and introduce identifiable meter numbers has drawn opposition from industry and civil society groups, amid concerns about affordability, privacy and the handling of personal information.
The Kenya Information and Communications (Amendment) Bill, 2025, sponsored by Aldai MP Marianne Jebet Kitany, seeks to make consumption-based internet billing mandatory. It would require providers to assign each customer a unique meter number, monitor usage, convert it into readable details and issue invoices based on consumption.

original_payload.original_title: Kenya: les effondrements d'immeubles rappellent l’urgence d’une réforme du secteur du bâtiment
original_payload.original_body:
Kenya: les effondrements d'immeubles rappellent l’urgence d’une réforme du secteur du bâtiment
Le Kenya, ces trois dernières années, a vu s’effondrer 72 bâtiments. Ce chiffre a été donné en fin de semaine par la NCA, l’Autorité nationale de construction, lors d’une commission parlementaire sur le logement. Elle a lancé une enquête, après l’effondrement de trois immeubles, lors de trois dernières semaines. Dix-huit personnes sont mortes dans ces accidents,
Publié le :  22/11/2026 - 07:57
2 min     Temps de lecture
Les forces de sécurité et la protection civile interviennent après l'effondrement d'un immeuble de plusieurs étages à Nairobi, au Kenya, vendredi 23 octobre 2026.        © Brian Inganga / AP
Par :
RFI
Publicité
Avec notre correspondante à Nairobi,   Gaëlle Laleix
Selon la plateforme indépendante StatsKenya, 38 personnes sont décédées dans 25 effondrements, depuis le début de l’année 2026. Susan Rutto, directrice exécutive de l’Autorité nationale de la construction, organe de régulation du bâtiment, ne sait plus par où commencer la liste de tous les dysfonctionnements du secteur au   Kenya  .
«  Près de 46 % des immeubles effondrés n’étaient pas supervisés durant leur construction. Les promoteurs démarrent les travaux, sans embaucher les professionnels nécessaires. Autre problème : les malfaçons durant le chantier. Quand un chantier est suspendu parce qu’il ne répond pas aux normes, les promoteurs ne le respectent pas et continuent les travaux. Et puis il y a la mauvaise qualité des matériaux utilisés  », énumère-t-elle.
La NCA se plaint du manque de moyens   qui lui sont alloués pour mener à bien sa mission de contrôle des chantiers. L’autorité n’est d’ailleurs présente que dans 27 comtés sur les 47 que dénombre le pays. Autre problème, soulevé par Joel Arumoyang, secrétaire principal du département d’État aux travaux publics : le manque de régulation des travailleurs du secteur bien que le pays soit doté d’un code du bâtiment.
«  Il y a encore des professionnels du secteur du bâtiment qui ne sont pas régulés : les architectes paysagistes, les gestionnaires de construction, les architectes d’intérieur. Parfois, sur les chantiers, ils se présentent comme ingénieurs ou architectes. Il faut réguler ces métiers  », affirme-t-il.
Un projet de loi sur l’architecture et l’économie de la construction a été proposé à l’Assemblée nationale en juillet. Il est toujours en cours de discussions.

Sports  NLNG Golf Classic: Falade, stakeholders tee-off as 250 golfers compete in Bonny
By  Philip Daniel Yatai   ·   16 seconds ago   ·  4 min read
✓
✓
By Victor Okoye
No fewer than 250 golfers participated over five days for honours in the seventh edition of the NLNG Golf Classic at the Bonny Island Golf Club, Rivers.
The Managing Director of Nigeria LNG Ltd. (NLNG), Engr. Adeleye Falade, alongside other dignitaries, performed the ceremonial tee-off to signal the commencement of the competition.
Falade described the tournament as an exciting platform for strengthening relationships and fostering closer ties between NLNG and its stakeholders.
He said the event also provided an opportunity for participants to enjoy the game while experiencing the hospitality and unique environment of Bonny Island.
“It is pretty exciting, and I look forward to events like this because they help us stay together, bond with our stakeholders and continue advancing the cause of our company,” he said.
Falade urged the golfers to enjoy themselves, have fun and make the most of the hospitality offered by NLNG.
The General Manager, External Relations and Sustainable Development, NLNG, Dr Sophia Horsfall, said the tournament provided an opportunity for guests to experience the natural and cultural attractions of Bonny Island.
Horsfall said the competition also offered participants an avenue to connect, interact and appreciate the environment in which NLNG operates.
She described the Bonny Island Golf Club course as beautiful, encouraging participants to take advantage of the tournament to strengthen relationships and enjoy their stay.
The Captain of Bonny Island Golf Club (BIGC), Michael Ukaegbu, said the competition attracted its highest number of participants in the last seven editions.
Ukaegbu said the activities began on Tuesday, with a children’s competition, followed by events for greenkeepers and caddies on Wednesday.
He said spouses and higher-handicap golfers competed on Thursday and NLNG partner staff on Friday, while the main tournament on Saturday featured guests, stakeholders and shareholders.
“We have more than 200 participants, and the total  is over 250. This is the highest turnout we have recorded for the Classic in the past seven editions,” he said.
Ukaegbu said the tournament went beyond sporting competition, providing opportunities for networking, business interactions and promotion of the NLNG brand.
He acknowledged the support of industry partners and organisations, including the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Ltd. (NNPC), Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC), Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA), Renaissance Africa Energy Company Limited, Total Energy, amongst others
The captain also appreciated the various clubs who accepted BIGC’s invitation to participate in tournament, including Port Harcourt Golf club, Python Golf Club, Arsenal Golf Club, Owerri, Ibori Golf Club, Asaba, Python Golf Club, TYB International Golf club, Abuja, SB Abubakar Golf Course Shasha in Lagos, to mention a few.
He described their contributions as important to the success of the event.
The BIGC Captain also commended NLNG’s management, particularly Falade, for its sustained support for the club and the tournament.
He said the company’s commitment had helped strengthen the competition’s reputation and attracted participants from different organisations and golf clubs.
The Lady Captain of BIGC, Mrs  Marytina Osuchukwu, described the NLNG Golf Classic as a special event on the club’s calendar and an important platform for industry networking.
Osuchukwu said the tournament enabled business leaders and stakeholders to interact, exchange ideas and share experiences about their respective organisations.
She particularly welcomed the inclusion of the children’s competition, describing it as an important step towards identifying and nurturing young golfing talents.
According to her, the initiative complements the club’s golf academy, which provides opportunities for children to develop their skills and grow into competent golfers.
She urged participants to enjoy the competition, remain relaxed and give their best, irrespective of the final results.
“Even if you do not win the competition, you are still a winner because you have taken steps towards maintaining a healthy lifestyle,” she said.
The Human Resources Manager of NLNG, Mrs  Judith Asogwa, described the Classic as a major sporting and social event that continued to attract attention across the golfing community.
Asogwa said the tournament brought together golfers, industry leaders and other stakeholders in an atmosphere of friendship, entertainment and networking.
She said the event also showcased the attractions of Bonny Island, adding that its lively atmosphere made it an experience participants would cherish.
“The NLNG Golf Classic is the place to be. If you have not experienced it, you are missing out on the excitement, hospitality and wonderful atmosphere,” she said.
The seventh edition of the tournament, which began on Tuesday, is expected to end on Saturday with a colourful dinner and awards ceremony.
The event features a series of activities designed to promote golf, strengthen stakeholder relationships and showcase Bonny Island as a destination for sporting and social engagements. (NAN)

Defence/Security  Nigerian Army honours 14 armour corps retired generals
By  Rabi'u Sani Ali   ·   8 minutes ago   ·  2 min read
✓
✓
By Shafiq Shehu
The Nigerian Army has honoured Lt.-Gen. AB Ibrahim and 13 other senior officers who retired from service.
Ibrahim and 13 other officers, including seven Major Generals and six Brigadier Generals exited the army on Saturday during a pulling-out parade at the Nigerian Army Armoured Corps (NAAC), Obienu Barracks, Bauchi.
The army honoured the retired officers in recognition of their distinguished services, sacrifices and invaluable contributions to the Nigerian Army and the nation.
The officers are Major Generals MS Ahmed; OC Ajunwa, JO Ochai, IS Ali, SG Muhammed and IM Jallo.
Others are Brigadier Generals S Ahmadu; VO Ita, UM Aliyu, AG Nura, T Isa, EB Barkins and AM Usman.
The army authorities described the pulling-out parade as a military tradition  symbolising honour, institutional appreciation and continuity.
It said the event also celebrated the enduring legacies of the retiring officers and their contributions to the growth and operational development of the corps.
Also Ibrahim said the ceremony was solemn and symbolic in upholding long lasting military tradition, and strengthening esprit de corps in the army.
He said the armoured corps had provided opportunities for the retired officers to served the army and the country with dedication, commitment, loyalty and professionalism during their service years.
“NAAC is not just a branch of the Nigerian Army but a way of life. It teaches leadership, sharpness, toughness and ability to make difficult decisions,” he said.
Ibrahim enjoined serving officers to be disciplined, professional, curious and committed by embracing innovations, values and code of ethics.
While commending the retired military officers for their gallantry and sacrifices, Ibrahim thanked their spouses for their support and understanding.
He enjoined the retired officers to carry the bond of army brotherhood as they enter into a new phase in their lives.
Ibrahim, who is the Chief of Policy and Plans, Army Headquarters, voluntarily retired after 33 years in service.
Born in 1970 in Kaduna, Kaduna State, Ibrahim is married to a wife and blessed with children. (   NAN   )
Edited by Rabiu Sani-Ali

items.title: NGO, PFN launch initiative to empower 100,000 entrepreneurs

original_payload.original_title: NGO, PFN launch initiative to empower 100,000 entrepreneurs
original_payload.original_body:
General News  NGO, PFN launch initiative to empower 100,000 entrepreneurs
By  Folashade Adeniran   ·   1 hour ago   ·  5 min read
✓
✓
By Uchenna Eletuo
The Faith Economic Empowerment Programme (FEEP), in collaboration with the Pentecostal Fellowship of Nigeria (PFN), has unveiled an investment and empowerment initiative targeting at least 100,000 entrepreneurs across different sectors.
The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the initiative inaugurated in Lagos on Saturday was designed to promote self-reliance, wealth creation, job generation and national economic growth.
It aims to harness the economic potential and resources within the Christian community while connecting Nigerian entrepreneurs with international business partners, investment opportunities and funding support.
Under its pilot scheme in Lagos, the foundation plans to recruit 20 participants from every participating church for specialised business training and capacity development.
FEEP, a non-profit organisation with international affiliations, also seeks to facilitate diaspora participation in channelling resources and investment opportunities towards poverty reduction and enterprise development in Nigeria.
The programme is designed to identify individuals with business interests and entrepreneurial passion and equip them with skills to establish and manage sustainable enterprises.
According to the organisers, selected participants will receive training from professional business portfolio managers in bookkeeping, business management, investment development and mortgage-related opportunities.
The trainees will also undergo certification and due diligence processes before being connected to potential international grants, business partners and other investment opportunities.
The initiative is expected to help participants establish businesses and create additional employment opportunities.
The event, attended by church leaders, diaspora partners, investment managers and business mentors, had the theme: “Unlocking the Economic Power of the Church”.
Speaking at the event, the guest speaker, Dr Olumide Emmanuel, urged the Church to move beyond religious activities and embrace practical Christianity.
Olumide said this would enable churches to address the social and economic challenges confronting their members.
He urged churches to embrace collective responsibility by pooling their resources towards wealth creation, employment generation and improved living conditions.
“Let us practise our faith and move from religion to a more practical Christianity by being one another’s keeper,” he said.
He called for a shift from denominational divisions towards the collective values and resource-sharing practices of the early Church.
“We must move from denominationalism to faith as practised by the early Church by pulling the Church’s resources together to create wealth, jobs and foster people’s well-being,” he said.
He maintained that the gospel of the Kingdom and discipleship should remain central to the Church’s message, with salvation as its ultimate outcome.
The Chairman of FEEP, Dr Alfred Tofade, described enterprise as a major driver of economic development in advanced economies, including the United States, United Kingdom and France.
Tofade challenged Nigerian church leaders to identify individuals with entrepreneurial abilities and interests within their congregations and encourage them to participate in the programme.
He said the initiative was driven by the desire to help Nigerians and local businesses overcome economic difficulties and achieve sustainable growth.
He explained that FEEP would provide a structured platform for harnessing resources within churches and connecting Nigerian entrepreneurs with interested foreign investors and business partners.
“Many of our people outside are interested in doing business here, but they are looking for a trusted platform to work with.
“FEEP would bridge that gap and link trainees with grants and partners abroad,” he said.
He added that the Church possessed the organisational structure and community networks needed to attract investment, support enterprise development and transform lives.
Similarly, the Chairman of PFN, Lagos State Chapter, Pastor Yemi Davids, described FEEP as an empowerment initiative designed to help churches extend their impact beyond spiritual development.
Davids said the collaboration between FEEP and PFN could provide a platform for attracting foreign capital and expanding economic opportunities for Nigerians.
He stressed that the Church must complement its preaching responsibilities with practical, Kingdom-based economic initiatives that improve people’s livelihoods.
According to him, the partnership would also emphasise transparency, training and due diligence in identifying potential entrepreneurs and connecting them with international business opportunities.
Also speaking, Prof. Pat Utomi of Lagos Business School expressed concern over the level of poverty in Nigeria.
Utomi noted that the country’s abundant human and material resources should provide a foundation for greater economic prosperity.
He called on churches to embrace their responsibility to promote values, integrity and entrepreneurial capacity needed to build a sustainable economy for present and future generations.
The FEEP initiative is expected to expand its recruitment and training activities through participating churches.
The broader objective is to build an entrepreneurial network capable of contributing to employment generation, investment growth and poverty reduction.
The organisation made recruitment forms available and provided an online registration platform through its website, www.feepgruop.org.
The initiative places the Church at the centre of a wider conversation about faith, enterprise and national development.
It highlights the potential of faith-based institutions to contribute to Nigeria’s economic future through human capital development, investment mobilisation and sustainable business creation. (NAN) www.nannews.ng
Edited by Grace Alegba

items.title: Opinion| Beyond the SPLM primaries: What young lawmakers must deliver in 2027

original_payload.original_title: Opinion| Beyond the SPLM primaries: What young lawmakers must deliver in 2027
original_payload.original_body:
As South Sudan approaches its first general election—rescheduled by the National Elections Commission for February 11, 2027—a systematic political shift is already underway inside the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement (SPLM). Across the country, internal party primaries for both state assemblies and the National Legislative Assembly have sent a clear signal from the grassroots: voters are ready to turn the page.
From Jonglei to Central Equatoria, young SPLM cadres have unseated a good number of long-serving political veterans to claim the party’s parliamentary tickets. Yet winning those primaries is merely opening the door, for walking through it into genuine governance is another matter entirely. Entrenched patronage networks, for example, will not cede ground without a fight. If elected in February 2027, this incoming cohort of young parliamentarians will carry both a rare popular mandate and the heavy burden of delivering where the old guard fell short.
Beyond wartime credentials: Delivering basic services
For more than a decade, political authority in South Sudan rested largely on liberation-era seniority. Wartime credentials served as the primary currency of power, creating a political culture in which historical sacrifice frequently insulated incumbents from accountability. For years, citizens were expected to swallow broken promises in deference to the past, even as basic institutions withered and public trust wore thin.
The ongoing SPLM primaries have shown that this old formula is running out of road. By rejecting established heavyweights in favour of younger aspirants across multiple states, grassroots voters have made it clear that historical prestige can no longer bypass institutional stagnation. A generation born during or after the liberation struggle views legitimacy not as an heirloom inherited from the past, but as a covenant renewed through tangible results.
Young cadres entering state and national legislatures owe their rise to community mobilization rather than political favours dispensed in the capital, Juba. Unlike older politicians cushioned from daily economic shocks by state privileges, younger lawmakers feel the pinch alongside ordinary citizens—from soaring food prices to understaffed clinics. To prove they are worth their salt, their immediate legislative priority must be basic service delivery: steering national and state budgets toward functional primary healthcare facilities in remote payams, rehabilitating feeder roads that link farmers to markets, and rescuing a public education system hanging by a thread.
Breaking the demographic and economic bottleneck
South Sudan’s long-term stability hinges on its ability to absorb a rapidly expanding youth population into a productive economy. With young people forming the overwhelming majority of the population, chronic unemployment is far more than a macroeconomic headache. It is dry tinder for local insecurity, cattle raiding, and political disillusionment. Young SPLM legislators cannot afford to treat youth empowerment as lip service or settle for token ministerial appointments.
Once in office, these lawmakers must spearhead policies that wean the country off its crippling dependence on volatile oil revenues. At both the national and state levels, that means legislating real investments in vocational and technical training across all ten states and three administrative areas to equip young people for trades, commercial agriculture, and local enterprise. Building an economy that works for the majority requires trimming bloated administrative overhead and putting money where it actually generates livelihoods.
Equally urgent is dismantling the gatekeeping that locks young entrepreneurs out of capital. Young parliamentarians should champion transparent, merit-based micro-credit facilities and agricultural grants free from political patronage, alongside civil service reforms that ensure teachers, health workers, and junior administrators are paid on time. When young citizens see a clear path to earning an honest living, the appeal of armed mobilization and zero-sum politics loses its grip.
Putting teeth back into legislative oversight
Past transitional parliaments have too often operated as rubber stamps for the executive, hamstrung by fragmented loyalties, repeated extensions, and lax oversight of public finances. Because many previous lawmakers owed their seats to political appointment rather than competitive elections, few were willing to rock the boat by challenging ministerial misconduct or questioning opaque budget allocations.
Entering the legislature with fresh grassroots legitimacy, young parliamentarians have a golden opportunity to restore the chamber’s constitutional role as a genuine check on executive power. Using parliamentary committees to scrutinize national budgets with a fine-tooth comb, demand audited financial statements, and summon ministries to account will be essential to curbing corruption. Accountability ceases to be an empty slogan when lawmakers insist on tracking whether funds allocated for a state hospital or rural road actually reach the ground.
Modernizing how representatives engage the public is just as vital to keeping the executive on its toes. By pairing regular constituency town halls with digital communication, younger lawmakers can pull back the curtain on legislative proceedings in Juba and state capitals. When citizens can clearly see how public money is spent and how their representatives vote, parliament shifts from a distant elite club into an institution answerable to the people.
Moving beyond ethnic politics
During the primary exercises, SPLM Secretary-General Dr. Akol Paul Kordit stressed that overcoming ethnic loyalties is central to transforming the party and uniting the nation. For decades, political elites have too often played the ethnic card to secure power, deepening communal fault lines and reducing national politics to a tug-of-war over tribal representation rather than shared prosperity.
Many of the young cadres emerging from these primaries belong to a generation educated in universities and towns alongside peers from every corner of the country. Having forged friendships, business ventures, and civic networks across regional divides, they are well placed to champion an issue-based political culture. Their everyday struggles—jobs, security, infrastructure, and education—know no county or state boundaries.
In state assemblies especially, young legislators will sit closest to the localized sparks of conflict, including cattle raiding, boundary disputes, and competition over water and grazing land. Cooling these flashpoints requires moving away from defensive ethnic solidarity toward community-driven legislation. By backing local peace committees, upholding both customary and statutory accountability, and investing in shared infrastructure that binds neighbouring communities together, young lawmakers can help build peace from the ground up.
From party tickets to real delivery
The primary victories of young SPLM cadres reflect a maturing electorate hungry for responsive leadership. Still, winning a party flag is only the opening chapter, and the real test begins after the ballots are cast. Once sworn into national and state assemblies, young parliamentarians will face immense institutional pressure to fall in line with the very culture of patronage and silence that their voters rejected.
Resisting that pull will take unity of purpose among the incoming cohort. Rather than acting as lone voices easily co-opted by seasoned power brokers, young legislators across party and regional lines will need to build issue-based caucuses capable of setting legislative agendas and defending constitutional norms. True political renewal happens not when fresh faces warm old benches, but when they change how power is exercised.
Come February 2027, these emerging leaders will not be judged by the veterans they unseated in the primaries, nor by the party slogans they invoke on the campaign trail. Their legacy will rest on whether they deliver where it counts—exercising fearless oversight, passing people-centered laws, and proving that generational change can finally move South Sudan forward.
The writer is a South Sudanese teacher, political analyst, and an SPLM flag bearer contesting for Lafon Constituency No.6 in the Eastern Equatoria State Legislative Assembly. He can be reached via  amajuayani@gmail.com .

items.title: Feature| From farm to market: New roads give Magwi farmers hope

original_payload.original_title: Feature| From farm to market: New roads give Magwi farmers hope
original_payload.original_body:
For farmers in Eastern Equatoria State’s Magwi County, growing food has not always been the hardest part of agriculture. Getting their harvests from farms to markets has often been difficult, with poor road conditions making transportation costly, slow, and unpredictable.
In some farming areas, vehicles have struggled to reach gardens, while farmers have faced difficulties moving their produce to main roads and eventually markets. The challenges have affected their ability to sell harvests, earn income, and make the most of their agricultural work.
Now, residents in parts of Magwi County say improved access roads are beginning to improve movement, raising hopes that the ongoing rehabilitation of roads will strengthen agricultural trade and improve livelihoods.
A section of the rehabilitated Magwi-Palotaka feeder road. (RT photo)
For Olaraga Simon Ogenga, a 35-year-old farmer, the difference is already noticeable following the opening of a community access road connecting farming areas to the main route.
“Before this road, movement was so difficult for us,” he said. “The vehicle could go from here to the farm, but when loaded with produce, we would get stuck on the way.”
He said the rehabilitated roads had made it easier for vehicles to reach farms and transport agricultural produce to markets without getting stuck along the way.
For farming communities that depend on selling their harvests, reliable access roads can determine whether produce reaches buyers fresh in good condition and whether farmers can earn from their labour.
Ogenga said the community had been motivated to open the road partly because of the difficulties farmers faced transporting goods from farms to markets. He added that the work also provided an opportunity for people without jobs to earn some money to support themselves.
The road-opening exercise brought together different groups within the community, including women, young people and other residents who took part in the work.
Among them was Aloyo Josephine, a 32-year-old mother of four and farmer, who said the community had been encouraged to participate because of the difficulties they faced moving produce from their gardens to markets and homes.
She said local leaders mobilised residents and organised them into groups that included youth, widows, persons with disabilities, women and men before work began.
Opening the road was not easy, particularly when residents had to clear trees and other obstacles. Aloyo said many of those involved in the labour were women, who worked for several hours despite the physical demands.
She also raised concerns about the payment, saying the amount received did not adequately reflect the effort and time spent on the work.
“Our payment was not good because we worked very hard for three to four hours, but our payment was little,” Aloyo stated.
Despite the difficulties, she said opening the access road had improved movement between farming areas, markets and homes, even before the work was fully completed.
She said the improved connection was particularly important for farmers who depend on produce from Palotaka, an area known for agricultural production.
According to Aloyo, residents in Magwi benefit from food produced in Palotaka, but transporting it to town had previously been difficult because of poor road conditions.
She said the rehabilitation of the Magwi–Palotaka Road, together with the community access roads connecting farms to the main route, would make it easier for farmers to bring their produce to markets and improve links between agricultural communities and consumers.
A cabbage garden in Pajok, Magwi County. (Courtesy photo)
The rehabilitation of the feeder road and the construction or improvement of community access roads form part of a wider effort by the government and development partners to address transportation challenges facing farming communities in Magwi.
Karlo Andrew Akwo, caretaker Minister of Agriculture in Eastern Equatoria State, said poor roads had long prevented farmers from getting the full value of their harvests, with high transportation costs and spoiled produce affecting household incomes.
“Our hard-working farmers have been producing abundant crops, yet getting those harvests to the market has been challenging due to road conditions, leading to high transport costs, spoiled produce and loss of income for families who depend on the land,” he stated.
According to Akwo, the feeder road will help lower transportation costs for agricultural inputs, including seeds and fertilisers, while making it easier for trucks and traders to reach farms and move harvested crops to markets in Magwi, Juba and other parts of South Sudan.
He added that improved access could boost household incomes and enable farmers to expand production and invest in their children’s education and healthcare.
The road works are being implemented under the South Sudan Livelihoods Resilience Program, a government-led initiative supported by the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD), with the United Nations Office for Project Services (UNOPS) providing implementation support.
The project is financed by IFAD and the Government of the Netherlands. Work on the 44-kilometre Magwi–Palotaka feeder road began in October 2026 and is expected to be completed in December 2026.
Caroline Mwongera, IFAD Country Director in South Sudan, said a recent visit to communities along the route had shown progress and some early benefits from improved road access.
She said residents had reported that the cost of transporting food from Lobone to Magwi had fallen by half, while women told the delegation that travelling to Magwi Hospital to deliver their children had become more comfortable.
Mwongera said rural roads were important because they connected farmers to markets, allowing them to transport produce, improve household incomes and strengthen rural livelihoods.
She also stressed the importance of maintaining the infrastructure after completion, saying local authorities and communities needed to work together to ensure the roads remained usable.
Petronella Halwiindi Kasaka, UNOPS Country Manager in South Sudan, said the rehabilitation formed part of broader investments in community infrastructure, agriculture and livelihoods under the programme, which is being implemented across eight counties.
She said the road investment was expected to reduce transportation constraints, improve farmers’ access to markets and connect rural communities to wider economic opportunities.
The programme targets 61,808 vulnerable households, representing about 370,848 people, through support for agriculture, cash-for-work activities and climate-resilient infrastructure.
For farmers in Magwi, however, the value of the roads will ultimately be measured by whether they can move their harvests more easily, reach buyers and earn better incomes from their work.
As rehabilitation continues, residents hope the improved connections between farms, feeder roads and markets will reduce some of the difficulties they have faced for years.
For Josephine and other farmers, the expectation is straightforward: that better roads will make it easier to move food from their gardens to the markets and allow farming communities to benefit more from what they produce.

items.title: Op-Ed| DEMOCRACY DIES IN DARKNESS: What Antalya’s overtime deadlock reveals about the world’s broken climate finance order

original_payload.original_title: Op-Ed| DEMOCRACY DIES IN DARKNESS: What Antalya’s overtime deadlock reveals about the world’s broken climate finance order
original_payload.original_body:
As the 2026 United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) closes in disarray in Turkey, without a U.S. delegation, without a binding adaptation dollar target, and with a starved Loss and Damage Fund, the Global South must turn from begging for loans to enforcing its legal rights under international law. When the 31st COP31 opened on the Mediterranean coast of Antalya, Turkey, on November 9, its co-hosts, Turkey and Australia, operating under an unusual joint presidency, billed it as the Implementation COP. Nearly two weeks later, as exhausted negotiators stumbled past their Friday deadline into bitter weekend overtime, Antalya delivered something far bleaker: a stark autopsy of a global climate architecture built to shield historical polluters while trapping developing nations in sovereign debt.
Consider the ledger left behind on the conference floor. In the final stretches of deliberations, revised draft texts stripped out explicit references to phasing out fossil fuels across 80 articles. They deleted an earlier proposal, championed by African ministers and least developed countries, to lock in at least $120 billion a year in public adaptation finance by 2035, even while the text itself acknowledged that developing countries need $305 billion annually just to adapt. Instead, negotiators reached for their oldest diplomatic sedative: another deferral, rebranded as the Antalya-to-Addis Ababa Roadmap, kicking the hard math down the road to next year’s COP32 in Ethiopia.
Most damning of all was the fate of the Loss and Damage Fund, hailed just three years ago at COP28 in Dubai as a historic triumph of multilateral solidarity. By the time delegates packed their bags in Antalya, the fund had received $2.8 billion in urgent requests from climate-battered nations, ranging from glacial floods in Nepal to droughts across the Pacific and East Africa, against just $486 million actually paid. The sole major new commitment announced during the summit was a modest €25 million pledge from the European Union. Meanwhile, the United States, historically responsible for 40 percent of excess global carbon dioxide emissions beyond the safe planetary boundary, sent no official delegation, having once again withdrawn from U.N. climate frameworks.
The core argument here is that Antalya’s deadlock was not an unfortunate diplomatic malfunction. It was the logical outcome of three decades of eco-colonialism: a legal and financial order that converts the historical ecological debt owed by industrialised nations into discretionary charity and interest-bearing sovereign loans.
The coloniality of the atmosphere
In Washington and European capitals, climate change is routinely framed as a universal tragedy of the commons, an accidental management problem to be solved by carbon markets and private sector innovation. Yet the chemistry of the atmosphere tells a different story. Between 1850 and the early twenty-first century, the industrialised economies of the Global North accounted for roughly 79 percent of cumulative carbon dioxide emissions and 92 percent of excess global emissions, pushing the planet past safe ecological limits. That fossil-fuelled wealth was neither self-contained nor ecologically innocent; as legal scholars have shown, Northern industrialisation rested upon centuries of colonial extraction across Africa, Asia, the Caribbean, and the Americas.
In effect, industrial powers colonised the global atmosphere as an open-access waste sink, internalising the economic surpluses of coal, oil, and gas while externalising lethal droughts, cyclones, and rising seas onto formerly colonised territories. Under the elementary principles of public international law, established by the Permanent Court of International Justice in the 1928 Factory at Chorzów ruling and codified in the International Law Commission’s Articles on State Responsibility (ARSIWA), a state that inflicts transboundary injury owes full reparation through restitution, compensation, and satisfaction.
Yet when developing countries ask for climate justice, the international financial order hands them a loan application. Independent audits show that roughly 60 to 70 percent of reported public climate finance from wealthy nations is delivered not as grants, but as interest-bearing loans. When a climate-intensified flood or multi-year drought wipes out bridges, hospitals, and harvests across the Global South, devastated governments are forced to borrow from the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, and commercial bondholders simply to rebuild what Northern emissions destroyed. Servicing those dollar-denominated debts forces austerity cuts and the accelerated extraction of minerals and fossil fuels, directly eroding the post-colonial principle of Permanent Sovereignty over Natural Resources enshrined in U.N. General Assembly Resolution 1803.
Five lessons from Paris to Antalya
The breakdown in Antalya did not happen overnight. It is the culmination of a 35-year strategy by wealthy nations to sever climate finance from legal liability. Understanding five hard lessons from previous COP summits is indispensable for any policymaker hoping to salvage multilateralism before COP32 convenes in Addis Ababa.
First, symbolic institutions cannot replace legal rights. When Vanuatu and the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS) first proposed a Loss and Damage mechanism in 1991, they demanded an International Insurance Pool funded by mandatory assessed contributions, calculated at 50 percent on historical emissions and 50 percent on national income, to compensate vulnerable states for sea-level rise. Twenty-four years later, at COP21 in Paris, developing nations won a standalone Loss and Damage clause (Article 8), but only by surrendering Paragraph 51 of Decision 1/CP.21, which declared that Article 8 does not involve or provide a basis for any liability or compensation. Ever since, wealthy nations have cited Paragraph 51 to treat climate restitution as optional philanthropy.
Second, housing climate justice inside the World Bank reproduces donor hegemony. After Pakistan’s catastrophic 2022 floods forced the creation of a Loss and Damage Fund at COP27 in Sharm el-Sheikh, the United States and Europe used COP28 in Dubai to place the fund under the interim four-year trusteeship of the World Bank as a Financial Intermediary Fund. They replaced mandatory verbs (shall) with voluntary pleas (urges and invites), permitted loans alongside grants, and imposed complex World Bank fiduciary standards that choke direct access. Antalya’s stark ratio, $2.8 billion in requests versus $486 million received, is the predictable verdict on voluntary World Bank charity.
Third, creative accounting masks the retreat from real finance. At COP29 in Baku in 2024, developing countries documented at least $1.3 trillion per year in real climate finance needs. In response, developed nations pushed through a New Collective Quantified Goal (NCQG) of at least $300 billion per year by 2035, a figure padded with multilateral bank loans and mobilised private finance, stripped of any dedicated Loss and Damage sub-goal, and paired with a non-binding roadmap to $1.3 trillion. At COP31 in Antalya, an early draft briefly proposed a breakthrough, asking the Standing Committee on Finance to count only the grant-equivalent value of loans rather than the full-face value, only for donor resistance to dilute binding finance numbers once again.
Fourth, consensus rules have become an instrument of paralysis. Because the UNFCCC has never adopted formal voting rules, a handful of fossil-fuel exporters or reluctant donors can strip core science and finance commitments from a cover text at the eleventh hour. As Antalya’s talks spilt past their deadline with fossil-fuel language gutted from the draft agreement, veteran diplomats openly admitted that climate diplomacy is drifting from doing by consensus to doing by coalition.
Fifth, the quiet retreat of traditional donors is colliding with physical reality. From U.S. withdrawals and slashed foreign aid to the Global Environment Facility’s lowest replenishment in two decades and adaptation finance stuck near $28–$32 billion against $305 billion in annual needs, the charity model has exhausted its credibility.
Why Washington Cannot Walk Away from International Law.
Here is the reality that U.S. policymakers and reluctant European treasuries must confront after Antalya: withdrawing from the Paris Agreement or boycotting a U.N. summit no longer buys legal immunity.
On July 23, 2025, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) issued a unanimous, historic Advisory Opinion on the Obligations of States in respect of Climate Change, reinforcing the May 2024 Advisory Opinion of the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) and the May 2025 appellate ruling of Germany’s Higher Regional Court of Hamm in Saúl Luciano Lliuya v. RWE AG, which affirmed in principle that major corporate carbon emitters can be held proportionally liable under civil law for transboundary climate protection costs.
The ICJ systematically dismantled the legal alibis that industrialised nations had deployed for thirty years. First, quoting Article 55 of ARSIWA, the Court flatly rejected the claim that the UNFCCC and Paragraph 51 function as an exclusive lex specialis shielding polluters from general international law. Second, the Court ruled that every nation on Earth, whether a party to the Paris Agreement or not, is bound by customary international law to exercise stringent due diligence to prevent significant harm to the global climate system, including by regulating private fossil-fuel actors. Third, it confirmed that international cooperation on adaptation and Loss and Damage is a binding legal obligation, and that breaches of climate duties constitute internationally wrongful acts triggering the full panoply of customary reparations: cessation, restitution, monetary compensation, and satisfaction.
The road to Addis Ababa: Turning legal rights into leverage
For all the frustration inside Antalya’s plenary halls, the summit also revealed the outlines of a post-consensus future. On the sidelines of COP31, seven countries, spanning both North and South, including Kenya, Spain, Tuvalu, and the United Kingdom, signed an open letter endorsing targeted polluter-pays levies on high-emitting sectors such as aviation. Simultaneously, 25 nations emerging from the 57-country Santa Marta process committed to publishing national roadmaps away from
fossil fuels, ahead of a second transitioning conference to be led next year by Tuvalu and Ireland.
Between now and COP32 in Addis Ababa next November, developing countries and reform-minded allies in the Global North should abandon the illusion that polite consensus will transform climate finance. Instead, they must pursue four decisive structural shifts:
Ahead of Addis Ababa, developing nations must reject any NCQG tracking rule that counts face-value commercial loans or private equity as public climate finance. Only pure grants and the net grant element of concessional finance satisfy legal obligations under Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement and customary law.
Rather than begging national treasuries for voluntary charity, the international community must scale the Antalya polluter-pays coalition into binding global solidarity levies on aviation, maritime shipping fuels, and wellhead fossil-fuel extraction, channelling automatic, predictable revenue directly into adaptation and Loss and Damage.
End World Bank Trusteeship on Schedule; in other words, the World Bank’s four-year interim hosting of the Loss and Damage Fund expires in 2027–2028. COP32 in Ethiopia must exercise its review clause to establish an independent, democratically governed U.N. fund that disburses 100 percent unconditional grants via direct national access.
When creditors demand debt service from nations devastated by climate disasters they did not cause, Global South finance ministries should invoke the 2025 ICJ Advisory Opinion to pursue coordinated sovereign debt-for-climate-loss cancellation and, where necessary, contentious claims under international law.
Finally, for decades, wealthy nations treated climate justice as an exercise in foreign-policy benevolence, something to be offered in small, conditional instalments when politically convenient, and withdrawn when domestic moods shifted. COP31 in Antalya proved that era is dead. Whether Washington returns to the negotiating table or remains on the sidelines, the legal and fiscal invoice for colonising the global atmosphere is coming due. Paying it in grants, not loans, is no longer an act of charity; it is the minimum price of a lawful, habitable world.
Dr Ayine Nigo is an author and lecturer at the University of Westminster, London, United Kingdom. He can be reached via  nigoayine@gmail.com .
